AWS got hit by an outage too. Here's why you didn't hear about it

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (868 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theregister

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If a service falls in the forest and nobody hears it...
  • My editor asked me this week "why is everything except AWS breaking?".
  • In fact, as they are wont to do, AWS spokesperson Patrick Neighorn got salty to a reporter about how unreliable Downdetector is when it started showing them as impacted.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If a service falls in the forest and nobody hears it...

My editor asked me this week "why is everything except AWS breaking?".

It's a great question! They haven't been in the headlines! In fact, as they are wont to do, AWS spokesperson Patrick Neighorn got salty to a reporter about how unreliable Downdetector is when it started showing them as impacted.

Recent findings suggest that if you'll permit me a small digression, this stems from a misunderstanding of what Downdetector is for. Historically the AWS status site was so hilariously slow to reflect the lived customer experience that some jackass (me) built a rewriter that sits at stop.lying.cloud to make it a smidgen more realistic. As a result, the question people are really trying to answer when they visit Downdetector is "my app just broke; is it my crappy code or is there a global event going on?" There are mitigations for both, but they look nothing alike.

AWS view crowdsourced reports of the form "the internet is broken, must be AWS" as a stain upon their honor. In fact, it's a badge of their own success, as "the internet" and "AWS" have become inextricably linked in people's minds.

But back to my editor's question, "why didn't AWS go down?".

It has been revealed that AWS now has 34 generally available commercial regions, of which two are at the moment smoking craters due to the Iran conflict. Each of these has hundreds of services that AWS offers to customers, of which a dozen or so are high quality, if I'm being characteristically uncharitable. They experience degradation in various ways, and they go largely unnoticed.

But on November 15, AWS confirmed an incident that disrupted 11 of those ~12 good services in their oldest and most important region, us-east-1.

At 3:05 AM PST, they stated that they started seeing sign-up errors, authentication complications, and connectivity issues. Five minutes later engineers were engaged. Not to be outdone, their status page swung into action after a leisurely coffee, and posted its first indication of an incident 93 minutes later. (See previous comments on stop.lying.cloud). The all-clear showed up at 6:53 AM.

It has been revealed that every site has downtime. Sometimes it blows up publicly, other times nobody seems to notice. Heck, AWS said in September that it had experienced permanent data loss in its two smoking craters, but after that news cycle passed I haven't heard a thing about it. I do think it's patently unreasonable to blame them for this specific problem; "acts of war" are kinda hard to predict from the corporate planning meeting.

It has been revealed that A few things combined to help AWS out on November 15. First, it was pre-dawn Pacific time on Sunday. Most of us slept through it; my kids aren't even up that early.

Further, the services that were most impacted (IAM Identity Center) were for engineers signing in to AWS accounts, not consumers staring at an app that stopped working.

Plus, the competition sucked all the oxygen out of the room: a day-plus Microsoft 365 364 outage and a four-hour nationwide air traffic ground stop had done a great job of level-setting what kind of outage was going to get attention, and "us-east-1 being weird but the apps still work" doesn't cut it.

Industry observers note that downdetector – which is owned by Accenture, so it's not like AWS doesn't have a throat to choke if they want to stop picking on reporters – measures consumer screaming. Originally, it was largely Twitter semantic analytics. This isn't a bad thing! As I said, I want to know if the internet is breaking. We can sort out exactly what part later.

Industry observers note that the November 15 outage didn't produce that kind of screaming. Ironically, the tool that AWS is complaining about in the newspaper is the reason they skated by without notice on this outage.

Counterintuitively, Downdetector reports that outages have decreased since about 2022. Instead, what we're seeing is large-scale centralization.

Our companies don't run email systems internally anymore; we outsource to large technology companies who are almost universally better at fixing and resolving large-scale issues than we will be internally. And it feels unkind to dunk on those hard-working folks for their outages; would we want them to dunk on us for ours?

("Wait, don't you own stop.lying.cloud?" "Do as I say, not as I do.").

It has been revealed that but whether anyone notices depends upon what layer broke, and when. If my company's email system broke on Monday, and your company's email system broke on Tuesday, the story would stop at "computers suck." But when everyone's email system goes down at once, the world takes notice.

It has been revealed that microsoft had to tell the whole world about a bug it mostly sat on since July. AWS hasn't had to tell anyone anything. My editor runs a tech publication that covers this stuff for a living and didn't know. You can't buy PR like this, and AWS didn't have to.

According to recent reports, if I were AWS, I'd stop complaining about Downdetector and send it a fruit basket. ®.

Apertus 1.5 Release Notes

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • Industry observers note that apertus 1.5 is a continued pretraining of the first generation model: adding 4 trillion tokens of text and multimodal training data to the 8B model and 2 trillion tokens to the 70B model, for a total of 19T and 17T, respectively.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, our latest release, Apertus 1.5, extends the 8B and 70B Apertus 1.0 models with image/audio understanding, an optional thinking mode, a four times longer context window, improved instruction-following, and better tool use. The updated 8B and 70B model weights were released to Hugging Face on July 24, 2026 under an Apache 2.0 license. Further details are now available from the project Technical Report, and summarized here.

Industry observers note that apertus 1.5 is a continued pretraining of the first generation model: adding 4 trillion tokens of text and multimodal training data to the 8B model and 2 trillion tokens to the 70B model, for a total of 19T and 17T, respectively. As with every Apertus release, the models are fully open: open weights, open data, open values, and full training details.

The full Apertus 1.5 training pipeline.

We introduce multimodality in v1.5 models in an early-fusion manner, where images and audio enter Apertus as discrete tokens in the same sequence with text tokens, instead of using a separate vision encoder. Images are tokenized with the Emu3.5 tokenizer (a 512×512 image becomes 1,024 tokens) and audio with WavTokenizer (40 tokens per second). We only extend the vocabulary, so the architecture stays unchanged and training runs at text-only speed. The models understand images and audio but generate only text.

Starting from Apertus 1.0, we continue pretraining in four stages:.

Overall, more than half of the training tokens are text-only, which preserves the language abilities of Apertus 1.0. The text data is refreshed with sources such as FineWeb2-HQ+, FinePDFs, and Nemotron-CC. All upcoming data, multimodal included, meets the same bar as before: publicly available, permissively licensed, and with robots.txt opt-outs respected retroactively. Every source is listed in apertus-data-transparency.

Post-training runs in five stages: SFT → long-context SFT → RL → DPO → charter alignment (SDPO).

Alongside the extended model capabilities, we also significantly expanded the scope of evaluations. Beyond the existing text-based evaluations used for Apertus 1.0, we added multimodal evaluations (image & audio), and thinking-mode evaluations.

The multimodal evaluations are done through MLLM-eval-suite pipeline, merging two major multimodal evaluation frameworks lmms-eval and VLMEvalKit. We also added a series of text-based benchmarks, as well as extended benchmarking for translation and multilingual capabilities, safety, and tool use. These can be found in our post-training evaluation repository, based on lm-evaluation-harness fork.

While still trailing frontier open-weight models, the latest release has also significantly improved performance in coding and instruction following capabilities with Apertus 1.5 8B outperforming similarly sized open-weight models on IF and multilingual tasks. Thinking further improves performance on challenging reasoning-heavy benchmarks like AIME. The multimodal performance of the model is closer to Gemma 4 12B and other current open-weight models. Apertus 1.5 multimodal performance is competitive in spatial understanding among open-weight models and document/chart understanding among open-source models.

We also thank our collaborators and external evaluators for their help with efficient benchmarking of Apertus capabilities. In particular, Apertus 1.5 highlights strong performance on Swiss Legal tasks, being on par with leading open-weight models (blog, code). Additionally, on Last Translation Benchmark, Apertus 1.5 8B presents machine translation capabilities which match GPT-OSS-20B and outperform models like Claude Haiku 4.5 or Google Translate (leaderboard, paper).

Apertus collaborates with the EvalEval Coalition to ensure fully transparent and reproducible benchmarking. We publish the Apertus 1.5 results in the Every Eval Ever (EEE) schema, a shared format that records not only scores, but also who ran the evaluation, how the model was accessed, the generation settings, and how each metric should be interpreted: details that are routinely missing from leaderboards and that often explain why similar-looking scores differ.

The results are shown in the Eval Card below, which combines the run data with benchmark and model metadata into one interpretable record, and are also available through Hugging Face Community Evals. This is the same infrastructure the UK AI Security Institute uses to publish its evaluations openly. Since our text evaluations run on our public fork of lm-evaluation-harness, which EEE supports with a dedicated converter, anyone can rerun them and compare their numbers against ours under identical settings.

Structured evaluation reporting also matters beyond research. EvalEval has mapped Evaluation Cards to AI governance requirements, including Article 55 of the EU AI Act and the GPAI Code of Practice, and found that the EEE schema can represent 56 of the 60 evaluation-reporting elements these frameworks call for. This fits how we already release Apertus: alongside the models, we publish a Public Summary of Training Content and, voluntarily, a Code of Practice document. Machine-readable evaluation records are a natural next step: making it easier for regulators, deployers, and researchers to find, interpret, and compare the evidence behind a model.

We are committed to promoting reproducible and transparent evaluation through Eval Cards and the EEE schema, and encourage other model developers to report their results in the same way, so that scores can be compared across models and organizations.

Industry observers note that all recipes, ablations, and data mixtures are documented in the Technical Report. We aim to popularize open model development by making the v1.5 training process public and accessible. Intermediate checkpoints are hosted in our Apertus 1.5 Hugging Face collection, including the base weights, SFT, RLVR and DPO, as well as our curated training data mixes/custom datasets in Apertus 1.5 datasets collection. Sharing them allows researchers to investigate how each stage changes the model behavior.

The report covers numerous ablations on the effect of post-training data in different stages, where we observed that the multimodal data mixed in together with text data during SFT helps improve across all modalities. We also find that the benefits of multimodal reasoning traces survive the subsequent text-only reinforcement learning: starting from an SFT checkpoint trained with multimodal traces, RL improves mathematics more than when starting from a text-only checkpoint, and the advantage on reasoning tasks persists throughout training.

Proton Lumo and Infomaniak Euria are two widely used apps that have recently integrated Apertus 1.5. These deployments are linked in the Community Showcase among others - see this discussion thread for a preview.

In a recent development, access to Apertus 1.5 in the form of an API for developers has been announced by a range of providers, including Swisscom, Infomaniak, Phoeniqs, and other companies listed in our General Availability guide. The report also provides details on how we work with external evaluators to test and prepare the models.

Technical instructions for running the models are in the model cards of the Apertus releases on Hugging Face and in our Quickstart guide.

Thank you for reading this blog post and being part of our community! We just celebrated five million downloads in our Hugging Face analytics 🤗 and are not slowing down. At the recent AI+X Summit in Zurich, our team revealed the roadmap for Apertus 2.0: sparse/MoE architecture, ~600B total parameters, extended training schedule, with agents, mathematics and coding as priorities.

In summary: we invite you to read our report, download the models, explore the intermediate checkpoints, finetune the weights, and reproduce our evaluations. Questions that are not already covered in our publications or website FAQ are always welcome, and we would also love to hear which topics would be most useful to the community for future deep dives.

If you build with or use Apertus, please fill out the Showcase form, and reach out through the options on our Contact page. We are looking forward to highlighting more work, learning what you are building, and hearing how Apertus can be improved!

Industry observers note that project Apertus, et al. “Apertus 1.5: From Open Text Models to Open Multimodal Reasoners.” arXiv:2610.15542. Preprint, arXiv, October 11, 2026. https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2610.15542.

  • The BPF verifier has historically worked by tracing every possible path of execution through a program, checking, at each instruction, that various safety properties hold.

It has been revealed that the BPF verifier has historically worked by tracing every possible path of execution through a program, checking, at each instruction, that various safety properties hold. This works, but it can result in an exponential increase in the number of states that need checking in programs with complicated control-flow. Alexei Starovoitov, one of the kernel's core BPF maintainers, has shared a patch set that substantially reworks how the verifier tracks states, in order to reduce the size of that exponential explosion.

Industry News: NixOS bring-up on an Alibaba RISC-V board

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2096 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Feyor

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In the process of scouring Alibaba for a cheap Versal devkit, I unexpectedly came into possession of a Zhihe Computing A210 RISC-V SoC.1.
  • Industry observers note that it’s a cool board: there’s a ridiculous amount of IO exposed by the baseboard, not to mention 8 cores clocked at 1.9 GHz is nothing to sniff at for a RISC-V CPU.
  • I decided to make this board into a NixOS build server so I could learn more about the state of RISC-V support in NixOS and to get some practice in Linux bringup.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In the process of scouring Alibaba for a cheap Versal devkit, I unexpectedly came into possession of a Zhihe Computing A210 RISC-V SoC.1.

Industry observers note that it’s a cool board: there’s a ridiculous amount of IO exposed by the baseboard, not to mention 8 cores clocked at 1.9 GHz is nothing to sniff at for a RISC-V CPU. I’m not sure I could recommend buying any RISC-V SoC currently2, but all these distros that are starting to support RISC-V need to run tests somewhere that isn’t Spike/QEMU.

I decided to make this board into a NixOS build server so I could learn more about the state of RISC-V support in NixOS and to get some practice in Linux bringup.

My complete A210 NixOS configuration can be found here; I confirmed sound, HDMI, Bluetooth/Wi-Fi, ethernet, and the GPU were all working, but YMMV.

Nix makes cross compiling to RISC-V a breeze:.

It really is that easy—building pkgs.hello will produce a bona fide RISC-V executable (you don’t even need a Nix file for one-off builds, just run nix build nixpkgs#pkgsCross.riscv64.hello). Some black magic in callPackage ensures that compile-time tools are built for buildPlatform and build artifacts are built for hostPlatform.

In the process of compiling over a thousand packages I only ran into two problems: a problem with rust-bindgen using the wrong version of clang and ministream not being properly configured for cross compilation, neither of which was specific to RISC-V.

That having been stated, I did run into some pretty bizarre OOM issues for some of the heavy hitters like Clang and GFortran. I was seeing >9GB memory usage per linking process(!) when compiling from x86_64-linux, which will swiftly exhaust all of your memory if you have max-jobs/cores set to sane values. I sidestepped this issue by temporarily nerfing build parallelism into oblivion and running the offending builds overnight:.

According to recent reports, I don’t (yet) have access to a RISC-V remote Nix builder, but even if I did, it’s substantially faster to cross compile everything from my desktop. Cross compilation can get a little wonky with Nix flakes because you have to encode the buildPlatform in the output schema somehow, but nixosConfigurations does not allow nesting (nixosConfigurations.x86_64-linux-a210 is valid, but nixosConfigurations.x86_64-linux.a210 isn’t).

My solution to this is to expose the relevant build artifacts of the NixOS configuration (ISO + flashing script) under packages.${system} by creating a “wrapper” NixOS configuration for each buildPlatform that extends nixosConfigurations.a210:.

This way nixosConfigurations is agnostic to buildPlatform, and cross compilation is straightforward—running nix build .#image on an x86_64-linux machine will use x86_64-linux as the buildPlatform, as one would expect.

Ok, so the goal is to boot U-Boot FSBL -> OpenSBI -> U-Boot SSBL -> Linux -> NixOS userspace, using the vendor’s Buildroot scripts as reference.

It has been revealed that using vendor forks of U-Boot/Linux/OpenSBI is a simple matter of overriding src and sprinkling in a few patches (almost always to fix compiler warnings that have been promoted to errors in the latest version of GCC/Clang in nixpkgs). All we really have to do is slot in the vendor kernel by setting boot.kernelPackages = pkgs.linuxPackagesFor pkgs.linuxA210;.

Armed with a bootloader and NixOS image, I plugged in the A210 to my MacBook and turned on Fastboot flashing mode, but to my dismay macOS refused to enumerate the device. Initially I figured the board was a lemon (due to it being a freebie and all), but I wasn’t ready to give up hope that easily.

I pored over the datasheet looking for alternative boot methods, and I investigated using PD resistors to force QSPI boot (using NORbert in lieu of a real QSPI device) to bootstrap into Linux userspace, at which point I could flash the eMMC directly without relying on Fastboot. But before pulling out my soldering iron I decided to try plugging the board into a different computer, which instantly detected the board. D’oh!

Ok, so Fastboot works3 and I’m able to load the flasher firmware and program eMMC (I based my Fastboot payload on openEuler’s A210 guide instead of the vendor’s script which flashes 7(!) different partitions), but after that I still got dead silence on UART. At this point I was pretty suspicious of my serial connection, so I decided to test it on a Pi Pico: lo and behold, it turns out leaving my BMP’s vRef pin floating was the culprit.

After losing several hours and my dignity to the aforementioned skill matter, I was greeted with the following panic:.

Judging from the above register dump, something seems to be amiss with OpenSBI itself:.

This confirmed my suspicion that the illegal instruction was from an ISA extension (in this case, a vector instruction). Initially I didn’t understand why this occurred: why would a CPU trap on an instruction it supports? I consulted the ISA spec and discovered that executing a vector instruction without the vector context bits of the mstatus register configured properly will result in the exact illegal instruction exception that I was seeing.

In a recent development, so roughly what was happening was the processor was context switching to OpenSBI where the vector context was not enabled, but certain operations like memset were optimized to use vector extensions because OpenSBI was compiled with -march=rv64gv. I conjecture that the vendor didn’t run into this issue because they compiled OpenSBI with a GCC toolchain that didn’t support vector instructions, but who’s to say? Backporting a patch that sets -march=generic did the trick, and now we’re making it into U-Boot stage 2.

At this point I could boot Linux from eMMC manually, but I wanted to take the time to do things “right”. I prefer the more generic distro boot to the hard coded boot command the vendor came up with, so I decided to roll my own board header.

According to recent reports, ok—now we’re able to get most of the way through the initrd before UART abruptly goes silent. Fortunately, the last message makes the problem pretty clear:.

It’s a bit of a hack, but I decided to set clk_ignore_unused on the kernel command line just to see if we could get more logs. Imagine my surprise when after reflashing, the board makes it all the way into NixOS userspace with no issues! Although I steeled my resolve to go spelunking in the device tree to find which clock was not marked as critical, I decided not to waste my time when I realized the vendor also sets clk_ignore_unused in their kernel cmdline. ¯\_(ツ)_/¯.

I would be remiss if I didn’t mention that running an old kernel in the current era of AI-assisted kernel vulnerability disclosures hitting LKML every other week does not exactly help me sleep better at night. I looked into backporting patches for Dirty Frag and co., but if the attacker has access to my tailnet I’m already cooked.

In a recent development, so now that I can SSH in, we’re done, right? Well, the vendor explicitly advertises support for Vulkan/OpenGL ES, so I decided I couldn’t call this finished until I brought up the GPU.

This requires support in both the kernel (a driver to talk to the actual GPU hardware) and in userspace (implementing a uniform interface like Vulkan over the device-specific API). For the former, The vendor opts to ship a kernel module with no source; a firmware blob (with a device tree to make sense of it) I can generally understand, but I don’t get shipping kernel modules, and here’s why:.

Kernel modules rely on the pertinent ABIs of the kernel being built against and the kernel the module will run on being nearly identical. If CONFIG_MODVERSIONS is set in your Kconfig (which it should be), the kernel will refuse to load a module if its vermagic (basically an ABI checksum) doesn’t match that of the running kernel. I’m using the vendor’s fork of Linux, so the vermagic matches exactly—so far so good.

Industry observers note that but comparing vermagics only checks for identical function prototypes; there are several Kconfig options that can change the size, alignment and layout of kernel data structures like struct module. Many of these are security or debugging related, and I’ve done enough kernel exploitation in my day to understand that there are good reasons to introduce this seemingly unnecessary binary incompatibility.

The upshot is I can’t use the vendor kernel module unless I massage NixOS’s Kconfig into producing a kernel that passes Linux’s ABI compatibility smell checks.

Sources indicate that while searching for an alternative solution, I was pleasantly surprised to learn that my GPU is already supported in upstream Linux and Mesa! In my naïvety I thought “great, we’ll clone Linux 6.18, run make -M=$PWD/drivers/gpu/drm/imagination -C vendor-linux/lib/modules/6.6.0/build modules and we’ll have a perfectly compatible driver!”.

According to recent reports, however, several changes in the DRM subsystem thwarted my attempt for a clean port, and in a fit of desperation (SLOP WARNING) I vibe ported the driver from the 6.18 kernel tree to an external module I could compile against the vendor fork of Linux 6.6. Adding a ton of code I did not write or understand is especially not good for software running with supervisor-level permissions; using this code feels like taping a “pwn me” sign to my back.

If you’re following along, I want to emphasize that my slop driver is only for using the A210’s GPU, and if you chose to use it you should first sic your own clanker on the source to make sure I’m not punking you.4 Alas, this is (in my opinion) still better than trying to use the prebuilt kernel module.

I was getting a bit fed up with the “compile-nix copy-kernel hang” loop, so I took a few minutes to setup a MCP server for Ghidra. I then tasked Codex (without Daybreak) with comparing the vendor-supplied kernel module with the slop that was ported from newer Linux.

The issue was identified and fixed within 3 minutes, whereas printk debugging and debugfs abuse got nowhere in several hours. Static analysis for the win!

After ironing out the kinks in the kernel side, we need to coax Mesa into letting us use it by setting PVR_I_WANT_A_BROKEN_VULKAN_DRIVER, after which we can successfully draw triangles!

OpenGL-rendered spinning cube textured with a particular book cover.

HDMI capture of glmark2-es2-wayland running under Zink (context for texture).

macOS USB support kinda sucks (I’ve encountered similar challenges with the Altera USB-Blaster III); if a device isn’t detected, try a different computer.

(In an attempt to update my USB drivers I made the generational fumble of updating to macOS 27, which makes Asahi Linux look stable in comparison.).

Never assume something works just because you think it should (trust, but verify).

The multitude of kernel configuration options makes kernel module API/ABI compatibility a pain; having source makes the problem tenable but still nontrivial.

Overall, this was a fun (if not unexpected) project. I have fond memories of designing a OoO RISC-V CPU with all the bells and whistles during my time at uni, so this nerd snipe was particularly gratifying for me.

According to recent reports, it’s a bit of a shame that this machine won’t see a lot of use, but I anticipate that will change as RISC-V adoption continues to grow. Also, I am still flabbergasted that NixOS is completely slept on by SoC suppliers; I eagerly await the day NixOS will eat Yocto/PetaLinux/Buildroot’s lunch.

It has been revealed that I paid a frankly too-good-to-be-true price of $1.2k for an Alinx VD100, and so I was disappointed but not surprised when I instead received some random $300 RISC-V curio. Thankfully I was able to get a full refund and keep the board; I think the “scam” here is to write off the cost of excess inventory as misshipments instead of surplus. ↩︎.

I’m loathe to recommend a Microchip product, but the PolarFire SoC Discovery costs $130 and doubles as both a RV64GC SoC and an FPGA. ↩︎.

According to recent reports, I couldn’t get the board to enter Fastboot mode after I flashed a bootloader, but this was fine because I could run fastboot usb 0 in U-Boot instead. ↩︎.

This is not to say you shouldn’t audit the other stuff too, but if you were pwned by something other than the PowerVR driver, at least you could take solace in the fact that a human (me) had the last laugh. ↩︎.

Sources indicate that to call this GPU “dinky” would be an understatement; for comparison, my RX 6700 XT scores 26230 on the same benchmark. ↩︎.

Welcome Beam: a 501B open model you can own, customize, and scale

📅 16 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3306 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, beam by Reflection is out on Hugging Face!
  • According to recent reports, beam is focused on coding and agentic use cases.
  • It has been revealed that beam has a native transformers implementation, as well as downstream libraries like vLLM and SGLang.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, beam by Reflection is out on Hugging Face! It is the first model from the new US lab, Reflection, and it’s open! It's a mixture-of-experts (MoEs) model with 501B parameters (23B active per token), supports text as input, has a context window of 1M tokens, and is released under the Apache 2.0 license.

According to recent reports, beam is focused on coding and agentic use cases. It is for teams that want a frontier-scale model on their own hardware, infrastructure, or cloud, and want to customize it to their own use cases. Beam ships with its own dedicated open source Rust based harness that delivers the best performance from the model.

It has been revealed that beam has a native transformers implementation, as well as downstream libraries like vLLM and SGLang. We’ve worked with the Reflection team to bring you inference, SFT (supervised fine tuning), and RL (reinforcement learning) recipes for you to build with this model for your needs. On top of day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM, this post reveals you how to run it, how to post-train it, and what we built with it.

Reflection is going to give out $10,000 Hub credits to the best projects that use Beam. All you have to do is make a thing, and share it on the Hub:.

It has been revealed that if you build something with Beam, then share it on the Hub for a chance to win $10,000. All you have to do is build the space, model, or dataset repo and share it on the model’s repo page. We’ll collect all the links, select the best, and send out the credits to your Hub accounts.

Beam is a text-only model built for long-context (1M context length) reasoning and agentic work. It is a sparse MoE model, where each token is computed by a small fraction of the network, so it runs at the speed of a much smaller model while keeping the capacity of a large one.

The decoder has 52 layers with a hidden size of 5,120. Most layers use sliding-window attention over the previous 512 tokens; every sixth layer, and the last one, attend to the full context. That gives 43 sliding-window layers and 9 global ones.

Inside the attention block (both layer types).

It has been revealed that the two kinds of layers handle position differently. Sliding-window layers use RoPE, since relative position matters most within a short window. Global layers use no positional encoding. Instead, each query is multiplied by a scaler that grows slowly with the number of visible tokens, (1 + (pos + 1) / 2048) ** 0.1. It acts as a temperature: the softmax keeps its precision as the context lengthens instead of flattening out. The implementation calls this scalable-softmax query scaling.

Sources indicate that attention uses grouped-query attention with 48 query heads and 8 key-value heads, with RMSNorm on queries and keys. A learned sigmoid gate, computed from the layer input, scales every channel of every head before the output projection.

The first 3 layers use a dense SwiGLU MLP. The other 49 replace it with a Mixture-of-Experts block of 256 experts, each a SwiGLU MLP with an intermediate size of 2,560, or about 39M parameters. The experts hold 98.4% of the model's parameters.

The router follows DeepSeek-V3's group-limited scheme. It scores all 256 experts with a sigmoid, splits them into 8 groups of 32, keeps the 4 best groups (ranked by the sum of each group's top two scores), then picks the top 8 experts inside them. Beam uses the same group sizes as DeepSeek-V3 but no shared expert. Expert outputs are combined with normalized router weights and scaled by 2.5.

Only 8 experts run per token, so the model computes each token with about 23B parameters. All 256 experts stay in memory, so deployment needs the memory of a 501B model but runs at the speed of a 23B one. The BF16 checkpoint is about 1 TB in safetensors format. The NVFP4 checkpoint stores most parameters in 4-bit precision for NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs, some parameters are kept in BF16 for accuracy. There are also FP8 checkpoints on the hub which are ideal for Hopper and Ampere series chips.

If you want to deploy Beam yourself, check out the vLLM or SGLang recipes below.

Recent findings suggest that the residual connections are the most distinctive part. A standard transformer adds each sublayer output to the stream with weight 1, so the stream grows with depth.

Beam counts the input embedding as step 1. At step k it adds the sublayer output with weight 1/sqrt(k) and keeps the existing stream with weight sqrt((k-1)/k). The squares of the two weights sum to one, so the stream stays at a constant scale from the first layer to the last. After all 104 additions, every sublayer output and the input embedding carry the same weight in the final hidden state.

Recent findings suggest that every sublayer is also normalized before and after, and the final logits pass through a tanh softcap at ±30, computed in FP32. The implementation fixes where it computes in FP32: the router, the SwiGLU product, the norms, RoPE, the query scaling and the softcap.

Hybrid attention works well for long contexts. Each layer caches 2 x 8 KV heads x 128 dims = 2,048 values per token. If all 52 layers kept every token, the cache would grow by 208 KiB per token. Only the 9 global layers keep the whole sequence. The 43 sliding-window layers hold a fixed 512-token window each and stop growing. So the cache grows by 36 KiB per token, roughly a sixth of the naive rate.

These numbers are per sequence, in BF16, with the transformers dynamic cache.

Here are the benchmark results across different precision levels, as provided by the Reflection team.

The most practical way to serve the model is serving the NVFP4 checkpoint, which retains most of the quality of the bf16 checkpoint. NVFP4 stores some weights in 4 bits, and this way, it shrinks the 501B parameters in BF16 from 1 TB to ~280 GB. Blackwell GPUs run NVFP4 natively but GPUs older than Blackwell like the H200 can't. The FP8 checkpoints are suitable for GPUs older than Blackwell.

A B200 has 180 GB of HBM3e, so two of them (360 GB) can hold the Beam weights, with little room left for activations and the KV cache. Strategy for four B200s (720 GB), which leaves plenty of room for long contexts and concurrent requests. You can also serve it on a full 8xB200 node, or on two B300s at 288 GB each, or even 8xRTX Pro 6000. If you don't have Blackwell hardware, use Inference Providers (serverless) to test Reflection.

Beam comes with day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM.

Install the latest version of transformers.

The easiest way to run Beam is the text-generation pipeline:.

The pipeline returns the whole chat. The last message is Beam's reply, already parsed by the response template.

Going one level lower, use AutoModelForCausalLM and AutoTokenizer.

Sources indicate that beam's tokenizer carries a response template. parse_response reads it and turns the raw output into a message dict, with the reasoning, the answer, and any tool calls in separate fields. This avoids the usual regex for splitting reasoning from answers from tool calls. And the rules ship with the tokenizer, so the parsed structure matches what Beam was trained to produce. The chat template can pre-write part of the assistant turn, which the parser needs to see.

In a recent development, pass tools to parse_response as well. Beam writes tool-call arguments inline, in its own XML-style grammar, so a bare 7 could be a number or a string. With the tool schemas, the parser casts each argument to its declared type.

Beam's config defines an expert-parallel plan. Expert parallelism puts each expert on one device. Attention, the dense layers, the embeddings and the LM head are replicated on every device. That is 8B parameters, or 16 GB in BF16. Load the model with a DistributedConfig:.

Launch the script with torchrun across 16 H200 GPUs. Each one then holds 78 GB of weights. With 8 GPUs each would hold 139 GB, which leaves no room on a 141 GB H200. The number of devices must divide the number of experts, 256.

Recent findings suggest that beam has day-0 support in vLLM. The command below serves the BF16 checkpoint with tensor parallelism across 16 GPUs (two 8x H200 nodes) and exposes an OpenAI-compatible API:.

For faster generation, add DFlash2 speculative decoding. A small drafter model proposes up to 15 tokens ahead, and Beam checks them all in one forward pass, so each step can accept several tokens. The cost is a little extra memory for the drafter:.

Both commands start an OpenAI-compatible server, so you can point any OpenAI client at http://localhost:8000/v1. For additional serving configurations, see the proposed Beam recipe for vLLM.

It has been revealed that beam also has day-0 support in SGLang. We recommend serving it with DFlash2 speculative decoding, which both commands below turn on. On Blackwell, the NVFP4 checkpoint fits on 4 B300s:.

It has been revealed that on Hopper GPUs, use the FP8 checkpoint on 8 H200s instead. Only three flags change: the checkpoint, the tensor-parallel size (8 instead of 4), and the attention backend (fa3 instead of trtllm_mha, which needs Blackwell):.

Beam is available on Hugging Face Inference Providers, powered by Baseten, Fireworks, and Together, with more to follow soon.

We are sharing some vibe evals of Reflection Beam-501B-A23B on five tasks, once each at low and high reasoning effort through the Reflection platform. These are vibe evals, not benchmarks. If you’re planning on using Beam, this is a great way to kick the tires and see how it behaves on specific use cases, and importantly, where it wins and loses.

Below is an overview of the prompts we ran and the output traces from the hub. The complete inputs, outputs, API usage, task fixtures, graders and conversation traces are in this public Hugging Face bucket.

Sources indicate that * Low's long-context response got all code behavior and all six source citations correct. However, the response did not correspond to the parsers format, so this is partly prompt ambiguity.

According to recent reports, † Low returned the correct answer, but omitted the requested justification. High supplied a correct roots-of-unity proof, independently reviewed.

Industry observers note that don’t take our word for it. Dig into the bucket, rewrite for your use case or project and push Beam to the limit.

You can fine tune Beam for your own use cases. Here, we share some examples in TRL and Miles to get you started on supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning.

The quickest way to adapt Beam to your own data is supervised fine-tuning with TRL's SFTTrainer. To keep memory manageable, we train LoRA adapters with PEFT rather than updating all 501B parameters: We used TRL’s SFTTrainer to adapt Beam to a simple goal: keep its reasoning in the language requested by the user. We fine-tuned on Multilingual-Thinking with LoRA, which trains a small set of adapter weights while keeping the base model frozen.

The setup combines model sharding at load time, expert parallelism, FlashAttention 4 and sequence packing. LoRA SFT fits on a single node with 8 B300 GPUs, reaching around 19,000 tokens per second. The corresponding H100 setup uses four nodes.

Industry observers note that after one epoch of Multilingual-Thinking, Beam reasoned in the requested language on 16 out of 16 held-out prompts, compared with 3 out of 16 for the base model. This small evaluation measures language adherence, rather than the correctness of the reasoning itself.

Training loss (left) and mean token accuracy (right) during a separate 500-step run on a reasoning subset of open-r1/Mixture-of-Thought, using one 8-GPU B300 node. These training metrics are from the official TRL example PR.

Reflection and RadixArk built a recipe that trains the model with GRPO in Miles, in BF16. You can update the full model or use LoRA to train adapters while keeping the base weights frozen. Megatron trains, SGLang generates the rollouts, and Miles publishes the new weights to the rollout engines after each update. We reviewed the recipe.

In a recent development, the recipe runs GRPO on DAPO-Math-17K and evaluates on AIME25. Build the image, download the data, and submit the job to a Ray cluster of twelve 8x H200 nodes:.

Industry observers note that sample: 32 prompts are passed to the model with 8 responses each. Two SGLang engines serve the rollouts on 16 GPUs each.

Score: the boxed answer is checked against the label, with a soft penalty for responses near the length limit.

In a recent development, revision: one optimizer step on all 256 samples. Group-relative advantages with truncated importance sampling, no KL or entropy penalty.

Train in parallel: tensor parallelism 8, expert parallelism 8, data parallelism 8, with sequence parallelism and full recompute.

Optimizer: Adam at a constant 1e-6. Gradients in BF16, master weights in FP32, moments in BF16. The optimizer state streams through node-local NVMe, so each trainer node needs 2 TB of scratch.

In a recent development, evaluate: AIME25 every five rollouts, eight samples per problem. A checkpoint is saved every twenty.

The next rollout is generated while the current one trains, so responses are one revision behind. Add --resume to continue from the last checkpoint. execute-colocate runs the same recipe on eight nodes, with every GPU training and serving in turn.

Industry observers note that you can also run GRPO with LoRA on four 8× H200 nodes: 16 GPUs for training and 16 for rollouts. The recipe trains rank-16 adapters on Beam’s attention, dense MLP, and expert layers while keeping the base weights frozen. Only adapter weights are synchronized with SGLang, and the optimizer state stays in GPU memory, removing the need for NVMe optimizer offloading.

Recent findings suggest that if you build something with Beam, then share it on the Hub for a chance to win $10,000. All you have to do is build a space, model, or dataset repo and share it on the model’s repo page. To inspire you, here are a few things we built.

At Hugging Face we love open and local models that run native to their hardware, but building native apps on Mac can be hard! Let’s see if Beam can help us out.

We asked Beam to build a native MacOS application that turns speech to text, and conveniently drops it at your cursor. We want to use MLX to get the most out of our Mac Metal and the Parakeet Model for great speech-to-text.

It has been revealed that we used Beam with the Pi coding harness to build the initial native macOS menu bar app, running Parakeet with MLX. The saved run includes follow-up prompts; the final source also includes later Codex repairs. The prompt above is a condensed version of the build requirements.

It has been revealed that you can check out the agent trace of how Beam built this in pi in this trace. If you want to try the demo out, download the source code or read the setup instructions.

Recent findings suggest that we wanted to see whether Beam could make faster progress by splitting a programming task across agents. We paired Beam with the open-source Pi coding agent and compared three setups: 1. one agent working alone, 2. five persistent peers collaborating through a shared Git repository, and 3. a lead agent delegating work to asynchronous subagents. The harness ran on Hugging Face jobs with inference through Reflection’s platform API.

For the tasks, we used ProgramBench: agents must recreate a program from its compiled executable and documentation, without seeing its source code or the evaluator’s tests. Each setup had the same 8M API-token ceiling and two-hour solver limit per task, shared across its agents. We saved implementation snapshots and evaluated them against fixed hidden-test suites from the ProgramBench-Tests dataset.

Our score-versus-latency plot shows the average fraction of tests passed. The time axis uses fixed reference rates for model tokens plus measured tool time, rather than elapsed wall time. We initially ran five tasks. The current figure shows a post-hoc subset of jq, xsv, FIGlet, and hexyl; ripgrep was excluded across all three setups because grading its saved artifacts was too slow. The published results retain all 15 original episodes.

You can inspect the runs in the Trackio dashboard, explore the published result data, and reuse the study harness.

Decision models are all the rage at the moment because they’re super fast and practical for many use cases. We started with Beam in Pi after Beam’s quota ran out to train and evaluate a custom decision model for developer incident triage.

We wanted to see whether a coding agent could turn an incident-triage policy into a small, fast decision model. The task was to read a developer incident and choose the responsible team, its severity, and whether someone should be pinged immediately. Using Unsloth, we fine-tuned Qwen3.5-0.8B to score these choices directly.

Recent findings suggest that first, the workflow built a synthetic dataset containing 2.3k incidents split by incident cluster for training, calibration, and testing. We trained a LoRA adapter and decision head for three epochs, with a 4-bit backbone, on one H100 80GB on the Science Slurm cluster.

For a baseline, we prompted the unadapted model with the full triage policy and ticket, without examples, and asked it to generate the three decisions as JSON. On the same 320 synthetic test tickets, the fine-tuned decision model got all three answers correct on 76.25%, versus 4.69% for prompted zero-shot. Mean ticket latency fell from 1,218.06 ms to 102.58 ms, an 11.9× speedup.

If you want to try out this experiment for yourself, check out the artifact bucket which contains the data, code, checkpoints and results.

Industry observers note that beam is a 501B open model that you can run on your own hardware and change. Start with the BF16 checkpoint, or try one of the quants FP8, NVFP4. If you build something with Beam, share it in the discussions tab.

Well why don't you build something that can run on cunsumer GPU like Qwen 3.8 Flash Next for example using strata ?

Recent findings suggest that that’s a good question. Apart from large corporations, no one would be able to set up this model in a way that allows it to function properly—it requires 8 RTX 6000 graphics cards, which would cost around 150,000 euros in total.

Recent findings suggest that thanks for sharing this! Small nit, but would you be able to add higher resolution diagrams for the model architecture figures? They come out pixelated for me (and possibly others) so I can't read the smaller annotations in the figures.

This is a genuinely exciting release — 501B Apache 2.0 with 1M context is the kind of thing that makes "open" in open-source mean something again. The residual stream design with the 1/sqrt(k) weighting is a nice touch; it's the sort of architectural detail that makes a real difference at scale without being a headline feature.

One question from the NLP side: the post focuses heavily on coding and agentic use cases, which makes sense for the target audience. But how does Beam handle multilingual text? I'm asking specifically because the 1M context window is exactly what you need for cross-lingual document understanding, and if the training data is skewed toward English + code, that's a gap that matters for non-English research communities.

Sources indicate that also — is the training data or at least the data mixture documented? For a model this size under Apache 2.0, reproducibility of the training setup is part of the open-source promise, and I'd love to see it.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Kristof Beyls has published a summary to the LLVM discussion forum to announce that the project is declaring success and bringing its relicensing effort to a close after eight years.
  • We've been asking past contributors to relicense their work since 2018.
  • According to recent reports, rather than trying to "chase the last tiny fraction forever" LLVM is winding up the effort.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Kristof Beyls has published a summary to the LLVM discussion forum to announce that the project is declaring success and bringing its relicensing effort to a close after eight years.

We've been asking past contributors to relicense their work since 2018. Upcoming contributions have come in under Apache-2.0 WITH LLVM-exception since January 19, 2019. Code contributed before that date was under LLVM's earlier licenses (UIUC/NCSA, plus MIT for some runtime libraries), so we needed permission from its authors to move it over. [...].

According to recent reports, rather than trying to "chase the last tiny fraction forever" LLVM is winding up the effort. Any contributors with code contributed before January 19, 2019 who have not signed a relicensing agreement and do not want their contributions made available under Apache-2.0 with the LLVM-exception can still reach out to the project to ensure their code has the appropriate SPDX license identifier.

According to recent reports, the LLVM exception to Apache-2 Posted Nov 21, 2026 13:13 UTC (Sat) by coriordan (guest, #7544) [Link] For anyone who doesn't know (like me until 5 minutes ago): The LLVM exception: https://merlijn.sebrechts.be/blog/what-is-the-apache-2-ll... It says two things. (Based on my quick read; corrections welcome) 1. That Apache-2 licensed compilers (which insert some compiler code into the executables they create) don't create Apache-2 obligations for the programs they create. 2. It fixes incompatibility with GPLv2 by saying that, for a combined work of Apache-2 plus GPLv2 code, if an authority decides that any clause of Apache-2 is incompatible with GPLv2 then that clause of Apache-2 doesn't apply. (Which I guess they decided is fine because the places where there could be conflicts, such as patents, using the GPLv2 version isn't enough of a problem to be worth incompatibility.) So, the LLVM exception looks like a pretty good instrument.

TorchNeuron: running HF models on AWS Trainium is easier than ever

📅 19 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (920 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • TorchNeuron provides a new native backend for PyTorch on AWS Trainium.
  • Recent findings suggest that torchNeuron is a PyTorch plugin that brings a upcoming backend for Trainium enabling support for eager mode, torch.compile and native distributed APIs like FSDP and TP.
  • 20, 2026, TorchNeuron will be available as a public beta.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

TorchNeuron provides a new native backend for PyTorch on AWS Trainium. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels natively support it, making it easier than ever to run models on Trainium and to share them on the HF hub.

Recent findings suggest that torchNeuron is a PyTorch plugin that brings a upcoming backend for Trainium enabling support for eager mode, torch.compile and native distributed APIs like FSDP and TP. Read the Pytorch blog to learn more about TorchNeuron.

Starting Oct. 20, 2026, TorchNeuron will be available as a public beta. Researchers and developers will be able to install it with pip install torch-neuronx.

To date, the Hugging Face experience on AWS Trainium and Inferentia — AI chips designed respectively for cost-effective training and inference at scale — has been delivered through optimum-neuron. This library relies on the torch-neuronx package, which is based on PyTorch XLA. It was the natural choice at the time, but it meant thinking like a compiler: lazy tensors instead of eager execution, static shapes only, a recompilation for every graph break. Optimum Neuron existed to hide that complexity, and maintained custom code (modeling classes, trainers, etc) to do so.

TorchNeuron changes this. It integrates directly into PyTorch and exposes neuron as a native device, with eager execution, PyTorch's own distributed primitives (DTensor, FSDP2) and torch.compile.

For the Hugging Face libraries, Trainium becomes a device like any other: Transformers, Diffusers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL run on it directly, with the same classes and scripts you would use on any other accelerator. From now on, we recommend that Neuron owners use these libraries directly instead of going through Optimum Neuron.

In a recent development, text generation is now natively supported in Transformers for a wide range of models. With TorchNeuron, 89% of the top 100 most-used text-generation model architectures are supported out of the box, compared to 46% with Optimum Neuron v0.4.5. You just need to pass the device_map=neuron argument in your code and your model will be moved to the Neuron devices.

It has been revealed that the following is an example of text-generation with tensor parallelism, which will enable to fully benefit from your Neuron instance. Note that it uses a static cache for generation as this is strongly recommended with Neuron to prevent frequent recompilations.

Recent findings suggest that now that Neuron is a native PyTorch device, training on Trainium uses the same Hugging Face libraries as any other accelerator: Transformers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL. You no longer need a dedicated trainer or a Neuron-specific fork of the model code. A standard TRL fine-tuning script runs on a Trainium instance with only a few Neuron-specific settings.

Here is a supervised fine-tuning script built on TRL's SFTTrainer. If you have fine-tuned a model with TRL on GPUs before, it should look familiar.

Parallelism is handled natively by Transformers. You put a DistributedConfig with the tensor-parallel (TP) and FSDP sizes in model_init_kwargs, SFTTrainer passes it to from_pretrained, and the model is sharded as its weights are loaded. The Trainer sees that the model is already distributed and does not wrap it again. You don't need an --fsdp flag or an Accelerate FSDP config.

Industry observers note that nothing in the script is tied to Trainium: the same code runs on any hardware. A few things are worth knowing when you run it on Trainium:.

The command below launches training with torchrun, which starts one process per NeuronCore. TP_SIZE and FSDP_SIZE set the parallelism layout, and their product is the number of processes: here 4 x 8 = 32, matching --nproc_per_node. The 32 processes form a 4 x 8 grid. Tensor parallelism splits each layer across the 4 cores of a TP group, and FSDP shards the parameters, gradients and optimizer state across the 8 TP groups.

We ran it on 8 Trainium2 chips (32 NeuronCores), which is half a trn2.48xlarge instance.

Industry observers note that training runs to completion, and trainer.save_model writes a standard Transformers checkpoint. Nothing in it is tied to Neuron: you can push it to the Hugging Face Hub as is and load it on any other hardware.

Industry observers note that many pipelines from the Diffusers library are compatible with TorchNeuron in eager and compiled mode. FLUX.1-dev, FLUX.2, Qwen-Image, Qwen-Image-2.1 and H3 are also compatible with tensor parallelism to make the most of your Neuron devices. The following is an example showing how you can use TP:.

You can run this piece of code with: NEURON_LOGICAL_NC_CONFIG=2 torchrun --nproc_per_node=8 run.py.

More and more pipleines will be compatible with TP. If a pipeline you like is not, you can also add support for it following this guide.

Recent findings suggest that make sure to check out the kernels from the Neuron team as more and more Neuron kernels will become available on the Hub to speed up your models. Neuron kernels can be written using the Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI), which gives lower control to optimize operations. This way, users can run their own custom operations and share them on the hub.

You can use for example this kernel to speed up your vision transformers with up to a x2.4 speedup on Trainium!

Special thanks to the AWS team for their work on TorchNeuron and for their reactivity to our feedback to make the HF integration as good as possible.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • I love using JJ and recently I’ve found a cool way to handle TODOs that works for me.
  • It has been revealed that usually I’ll put them in a TODO.md file which is pretty standard.
  • JJ has a cool feature where you can make empty changes, and even write descriptions for them before actually doing work.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I love using JJ and recently I’ve found a cool way to handle TODOs that works for me.

It has been revealed that usually I’ll put them in a TODO.md file which is pretty standard. But, I forget about this file quickly and am not very good at remembering to cross stuff off. Also since it’s in-tree I’ll often not want to update it, and then forget to do so later.

JJ has a cool feature where you can make empty changes, and even write descriptions for them before actually doing work. So what if I just make all the stuff I wanna do later as empty commits?

It has been revealed that pretty nice! When I want to start working on something I’ll rebase it out of my TODO tree and onto some other change.

I need to rebase my “TODO base” forward when i make changes, but because it’s empty it will never have conflicts and can pretty easily move around.

TODOs that depend on other TODOs also naturally fit here, I just make new empty commits on top of other empty commits.

It has been revealed that I have git.private-commits configured to make sure nothing with the private: prefix will get pushed. This ensures my TODOs stay on my local system. Of course, there are benefits to not doing this.

Anyway that’s about it, not very ground breaking but something I like.

  • If you run models on a Mac with transformers, diffusers or tools like ComfyUI, here's what 2.15 changes in practice:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you run models on your Mac or use MPS as your primary acceleration tool for computing, there's plenty to look forward to in PyTorch 2.15! FP8 arrives on MPS, language-model decoding gets faster paths through linear layers and softmax and fresh Metal kernels tackle some surprisingly expensive parts of audio, video and training workloads.

In a recent development, A quick word about who we are: we're the PyTorch team at Hugging Face. We contribute across PyTorch, and one of our focus areas is the MPS backend, where the goal is to make your Mac a first-class place to run and train PyTorch models. At the start of 2026, running even small models on MPS often meant working around unsupported operations, performance cliffs and unexpected memory growth. So we run real models from the Hugging Face Hub across language, image and video, find where MPS falls short and fix it upstream in PyTorch, more and more often by replacing MPSGraph with dedicated Metal kernels. Much of this post is the result of that work, done together with the PyTorch maintainers and community contributors.

If you run models on a Mac with transformers, diffusers or tools like ComfyUI, here's what 2.15 changes in practice:.

You'll need an Apple silicon Mac with macOS 15 or later and Python 3.11 or later (see the 2.15 compatibility matrix). If your OS is too old or no Metal GPU is available, the MPS availability check now tells you why.

To try the release candidate in a separate environment:.

Sources indicate that FP8 gives you another way to save memory on your Mac. PyTorch 2.15 adds torch.float8_e4m3fn tensors on MPS: one byte per value, half the storage of FP16 or BF16.

You can multiply these tensors with F.scaled_mm, which supports both tensorwise and rowwise scaling. Here's a small example with one scale per tensor:.

Industry observers note that every LLM has a prefill phase and a decode phase. During decode, each new token goes through the model as a single row, so the significant matrix multiplications turn into matrix-vector products. PyTorch 2.15 speeds up both kinds of layers that dominate this step: dense linear layers and mixture-of-experts layers.

It has been revealed that MPS has had GEMV kernels for torch.mm since 2.14, but F.linear still went through MPSGraph. PyTorch 2.15 connects them to F.linear, so the common [1, 1, hidden_size] decoding input uses them directly, with eligible bias additions fused in. Across 96 BF16 layer shapes from real models, that's a 1.23× geometric-mean speedup. The biggest wins land on small projections, such as the gates in MoE models, where the old path left most of the memory bandwidth unused. Large layers and LM heads were already close to bandwidth-bound, so they stay near 1×.

A mixture-of-experts layer sends different numbers of tokens to each expert. Grouped matmul handles those uneven groups in a single operation, and 2.15 gives MPS a native implementation.

In 2.14, grouped matmul copied the group offsets to the CPU and looped over the groups. The upcoming Metal kernels read the offsets directly on the GPU, using Metal Performance Primitives where available and a separate Metal path elsewhere. Small groups, the common case during decoding, get their own kernel as well.

For example, 64 tokens can be split into groups of 16, 32, and 16:.

Industry observers note that the decoding kernel shows up directly in token throughput. On an M3 Ultra with torch.compile, MoE models generate about 1.3× more tokens per second:.

Working with complex tensors gets easier. complex64 LU factorization, LU solve and triangular solve now run on MPS, which also unlocks the operations and gradients built on them, such as complex determinants. Here's a small system solved directly on the GPU:.

Sources indicate that small matrices get fast kernels too. For camera geometry and image transformations, batches of FP32 matrices up to 4 × 4 are inverted in a single Metal kernel that combines factorization and solving. Larger problems get attention as well: QR uses blocked updates, and triangular solves turn much of their work into efficient matrix multiplication.

Gated DeltaNet workloads get a dedicated fast path for batches of 16 × 16, 32 × 32 and 64 × 64 FP32 triangular systems with at least eight right-hand sides.

In a recent development, SVD is also more robust at numerical extremes. It now correctly handles very small singular values, very large or very small input magnitudes and basis completion with full_matrices=True, which in turn makes pseudoinverse and least-squares results more reliable.

It has been revealed that audio models, video decoders and training loops have their own expensive operations. This release gives several of them new paths through Metal:.

According to recent reports, token sampling gets faster in 2.15 as well. softmax and log_softmax now run on dedicated Metal kernels, and large vocabularies benefit the most: an FP32 softmax over a [1, 128256] row of logits drops from 57 µs to 7 µs, about 8× faster than the MPSGraph version. The speedup holds across other common vocabulary sizes:.

In a recent development, one of the most striking results in this release comes from the constant-padding change. The VAE decode in Wan-AI/Wan2.2-TI2V-5B-Diffusers makes 8,764 padding calls over a full 28-tile decode. With padding on Metal, peak driver memory drops from about 270 GiB to 8 GiB:.

You can now pick which MPS stream runs your work, directly from Python. torch.mps.Stream and the torch.mps.stream context manager provide the interface, and Tensor.record_stream lets the allocator track a tensor's use on another stream.

Here's a small example that sends work to a separate stream and synchronizes before reading the result:.

In a recent development, several more operations now run on MPS: torch.frexp, torch.logspace, torch.take and Tensor.put_, torch.heaviside, torch.special.laguerre_polynomial_l and unsigned-integer comparisons. logspace doesn't yet support integer or boolean outputs with more than one element.

Attention gets a correctness fix too: the MPS math implementation of scaled dot-product attention now handles batch and head broadcasting correctly.

Work on 2.16 is already well underway. Some of the changes below have landed on main and are available in the nightlies; others are still in review, so details may change before the release.

Sources indicate that once a model's decode path no longer contains any MPSGraph ops, the GPU only starts on a token after the CPU has finished encoding all of its kernels. PyTorch 2.16 commits the command buffer every 16 kernels, so the GPU gets to work while the CPU is still encoding the rest. For compiled BF16 decoding at a 2048-token context:.

Scaled dot-product attention is dropping MPSGraph completely: every shape will run on Metal kernels, with dedicated vector kernels for decoding and Metal Performance Primitives for half-precision prefill on newer macOS versions. The shapes that used to fall back to MPSGraph benefit the most. On an M5 Pro, decoding with grouped-query attention (32 query heads, 8 KV heads, head dim 80, 4K context) drops from 465 µs to 65 µs, and a 4K × 4K prefill with head dim 40 goes from 42 ms to 6 ms.

The move away from MPSGraph continues. Batch norm forward and backward are in progress, while MSE loss (up to 12× faster on small inputs), std_mean and var_mean (up to 4× faster) and bincount have already landed. bincount is the most dramatic: when most values fall into a single bin, counting 4 million integers used to take 6.8 seconds and now takes half a millisecond.

Bundled shaders will build for Metal 3.1 by default, with Metal 4 versions compiled only for the kernels that need them. That shrinks libtorch_cpu.dylib by about 25%, from 384 MiB to 287 MiB, and lays the groundwork for Metal 4.1 shaders with faster matmuls and native FP8 matrix multiplication.

Sources indicate that pyTorch 2.15 brings FP8 to the Mac, faster LLM decoding for dense and MoE models, more linear algebra on the GPU and a long list of operations moved from MPSGraph to dedicated Metal kernels. Give the release candidate a try!

A big thank you to Nikita Shulga, Kurt Mohler and Aaron Gokaslan for reviewing much of this work, and to everyone who contributed to MPS in this release.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News QCon San Francisco 2026: Scaling Tech by Aligning Humans.

Nov 21, 2026 3 min read.

At QCon San Francisco 2026, Scott Behrens, Principal Security Engineer at Netflix, presented how staff-plus engineers can define and align a firm-wide technical strategy. Drawing on Netflix's experience scaling internal AI agents, the talk argued that a strategy that brings people together can often scale impact further than any code an engineer could write alone.

Behrens explained that the work started when several product strategies, each with its own direction, began to share similar technical risks. Without a common technical strategy underneath them, teams were optimizing locally for different goals. His view was that technical strategy can complement product strategy without waiting for it, that lightweight strategies deliver faster than long technical documents, and that a clear north star does more steering than people expect.

In a recent development, the talk presented a playbook organized as levels in a video game. The first step is finding the right problem. Behrens suggested looking at tech giant communications, incident trends, technical debt, conversations with other tech leads, and gaps between team charters, then deciding whether the problem is worth solving now, whether it is foundational or compounding, and whether one is the right person to lead it.

Industry observers note that next comes the pitch. Behrens recommended a short problem statement that explains the intent, the expected value, the problems with supporting evidence, why the work matters now, and dated next steps. He suggested leaving possible approaches open so the people who join can shape them, and testing the statement early with a few colleagues, including the likeliest dissenter.

The presentation then covered building a small tiger team focused on creating the strategy rather than executing it. Behrens highlighted the importance of mixing perspectives, choosing people comfortable with ambiguity, getting manager support, and agreeing on scope, timeline, and a clear stop condition from the start. He shared that his first meeting had far too many people and still missed key functions, and emphasized that the most key trait of a good team is making it safe to push back.

Sources indicate that with a team in place, the next step is a north star, a short aspirational statement that gives direction and helps answer whether a piece of work moves the organization closer or farther from its goal. Behrens noted that writing a good north star is harder than it looks, and recommended drafting it with the team and pairing it with key outcomes that define what must be true.

The strategy itself, according to Behrens, is simply a set of choices. He described writing strategy bets as a choice versus another reasonable choice, naming the tradeoff explicitly, keeping each bet short, and revisiting them over time. If a bet does not feel a little uncomfortable, he mentioned, it is probably not a real bet. Keeping only a small set of active bets helps the strategy stay focused.

The talk also emphasized communication and feedback. Behrens suggested expanding support gradually from the immediate team to managers, directors, and executives, recruiting champions across the organization, and openly showing how feedback changed the strategy. Success, he noted, is when you are not in the room and people can still explain the work. He also reviewed common failure modes, such as unclear problem statements, the wrong team, vague north stars, bets that are not really bets, and strategies that nobody knows exist.

Recent findings suggest that the presentation concluded by encouraging engineers to keep strategy simple, communicate it widely, use a short north star to steer decisions, and adapt the playbook to their own context. As organizations launch more initiatives in parallel, especially around AI, the ability of senior engineers to align many teams around a shared technical direction may become as valuable as the systems they build.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, boodleBox says Montana has approved it as a vendor in the state’s Master AI Products and Services procurement program. The selection gives eligible agencies, colleges and universities a route to purchase the collaborative AI workspace. It does not mean those institutions have placed orders, deployed the product or agreed to use it across the state.

It has been revealed that the announcement is an example of a shift from individual employees experimenting with AI to institutions deciding what they can buy and how staff can use it. A department trying a chatbot may be able to start quickly. A public agency or university choosing an institutional service has more to decide: what data may enter the system, which staff can use it, what needs human review and who can see shared work.

Montana’s September information technology board report states its statewide AI solicitation closed with 50 vendors approved. The state estimates that buying from the resulting list can avoid roughly six months of procurement time per solicitation. That is the state’s estimate for the framework, not a measurement of savings from BoodleBox or a promise that any particular order will go through in six months less.

In a recent development, boodleBox’s announcement identifies the manufacturer as one of the approved vendors. It did not disclose a purchase value, the number of seats or a deployment schedule. Those distinctions matter because being eligible to sell gives the company access to a purchasing channel, but does not establish actual demand for its software. Montana’s procurement office describes eMACS as the state’s system for managing vendor registration, bids and contracts.

In a recent development, boodleBox’s product documentation describes a shared workspace in which consumers can choose from different providers’ models or let the software select one. People can also bring several models into the same conversation. A team could, for example, ask one model to summarize a nonconfidential document and ask another to identify omissions. Those responses are starting points for human review, not independent verification of the document.

Coach Mode adds advice about how to frame a prompt or evaluate a response. Memory Mode can bring information from earlier chats into an answer, while a human-only messaging option lets participants discuss a problem without sending each message to a model. These controls address different needs: a training group might want suggestions to follow an answer, while a team deliberating over an internal decision may want an ordinary conversation. Default settings and sharing permissions determine whether those distinctions are easy for staff to maintain.

BoodleBox says its security and privacy practices distinguish between manufacturer-controlled models and those run by outside providers. In the latter case, prompts and relevant excerpts of attached material may be sent to an outside API, subject to the company’s stated data-handling rules. An institution still needs to assess what can be submitted to each model, how records are retained and whether its agreements address the kinds of information staff handle.

A practical pilot would begin with low-risk tasks and measure both usage and the quality of the result. A university might track how much time staff save drafting course materials, while an agency might count how often a model summary needs substantive correction. The vendor list makes purchasing more straightforward. Whether the software is useful and safe for a specific workflow remains a decision for the institution using it.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Last November, we introduced AnyLanguageModel on this blog: a drop-in replacement for Apple's Foundation Models framework that lets you choose the model and provider your app uses. We heard from app developers who were curious about local models but weren't always sure how to get started. They also wanted to avoid the added complexity of supporting multiple inference providers. AnyLanguageModel grew out of that feedback.

Local and hosted inference each have their strengths, and both have a role in building this new generation of intelligent apps. A shared API makes it easier to choose the right model for each task.

A year and dozens of releases later, AnyLanguageModel 1.0 is out, along with swift-huggingface 1.0 and swift-xet 1.0.

Here's what changed, and what's next:.

Sources indicate that the core idea of AnyLanguageModel remains the same: use the Foundation Models API with the model that fits your app. To get started, change your import statement:.

The same session code then works with the system model, with open-weight models through llama.cpp, MLX, and Core ML, and with the hosted providers below.

Over the past year, we've added several major features:.

On OS 27, AnyLanguageModel also works with any model that conforms to Foundation Models' LanguageModel protocol, including Core AI models.

Alongside AnyLanguageModel, we've built out swift-huggingface and swift-xet to bring accelerated model downloads from the Hub to Swift apps.

Recent findings suggest that support for hosted models expanded this year, too. AnyLanguageModel now supports:.

With Inference Providers, you can use open-weight models that are too significant to run on the device with the same session code:.

Hosted providers get the same features as local models: guided generation, tool calling with streaming, and token usage on responses.

Reasoning is now part of the transcript too. When you switch providers, reasoning blocks are automatically omitted from requests if the newly introduced provider can't replay them.

In a recent development, API keys come from a closure instead of a string, so your app can fetch short-lived tokens from your own server. The README explains when to let people bring their own keys and when to route requests through a proxy.

AnyLanguageModel also runs on Linux, so the same code can work on a server.

According to recent reports, while we've made local models easier to use, the models themselves have become more capable, making the small ones a good place to start. Here are some of the most downloaded models on the Hub right now:.

Sources indicate that the first two fit on an iPhone, and Qwen3.8 27B runs on a Mac with 32 GB of memory or more. Selecting the MLX model takes one line:.

In a recent development, and if you have four maxed-out Mac Studios handy, GLM-5.3 from Z.ai takes about 1.5 TB in BF16. For the rest of us, it's available through Inference Providers.

If you're upgrading an existing app, see the migration guidance in the AnyLanguageModel, swift-huggingface, and swift-xet release notes for help updating your code.

Sources indicate that community feedback and contributions have shaped several of our major features. Thank you to everyone who contributed for helping make AnyLanguageModel more useful to app developers.

Industry observers note that language models have proven to be a powerful tool for building intelligence into products. They're also one of many kinds of models developers can put to work. We're excited to bring the same approach to more capabilities: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of models running on the device. Coming soon: models that decide, and models that listen.
