💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that andrew Nassar is CTO of IC Realtime, where he has helped guide the tech giant through shifts from analog cameras to digital recording, remote monitoring, and AI-assisted video analysis.
  • It has been revealed that IC Realtime designs video surveillance systems and software for residential and commercial environments.
  • You’ve helped lead IC Realtime through the transitions from analog cameras to digital recording, remote monitoring, and now AI.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that andrew Nassar is CTO of IC Realtime, where he has helped guide the tech giant through shifts from analog cameras to digital recording, remote monitoring, and AI-assisted video analysis. With more than 20 years in the surveillance industry, he focuses on turning advances in computer vision and edge computing into practical tools for understanding events, finding footage, and improving security operations.

It has been revealed that IC Realtime designs video surveillance systems and software for residential and commercial environments. Its Bunker platform adds AI analysis to compatible camera systems through a dedicated NVIDIA Jetson-powered gateway, supporting contextual alerts and natural-language video search. The platform combines local analysis with cloud-connected services for remote access and video history.

You’ve helped lead IC Realtime through the transitions from analog cameras to digital recording, remote monitoring, and now AI. What convinced you that AI could fundamentally change surveillance, and what advances have made sophisticated video analysis practical at the edge?

We have worked with machine learning and computer vision on our cameras for years. The opportunity became much more useful when the system could help someone understand an event and find the relevant footage, rather than simply produce more video to review. A homeowner wants to know what deserves attention. A business wants to find an incident without spending hours searching.

Bunker brings that approach to a dedicated NVIDIA Jetson gateway at the property. Moving core analysis closer to the cameras can reduce the dependence on sending every analytical task to the cloud and improve responsiveness. The practical advance is the combination of local computing and software that turns video into contextual alerts and searchable events.

My standard is still proven value. The technology has to solve a real problem in the environment where the customer will use it. A good demonstration is the beginning of that process.

Using Bunker as an example, could you walk us through what happens between a camera capturing an event and a user receiving an alert? Which AI functions run locally, what still requires the cloud, and what data leaves the property?

At a high level, a compatible camera sends video to the Bunker Gateway, and core AI analysis happens on that gateway at the property. The platform links detected activity to video events and can send a contextual alert with a snapshot and a plain-language description. The user can then review the video in the app.

Industry observers note that bunker uses a hybrid architecture. Cloud connectivity supports remote access, subscription services and video history, so it would be misleading to call the platform cloud-free or to say no video leaves the property. What matters is how that data is protected when it does leave. Everything is encrypted in transit, including live video, which stays encrypted from the gateway all the way to the viewer’s screen. The infrastructure in between relays it but can’t watch it. Each gateway authenticates with its own certificate, never shared credentials, and footage stored in the cloud is encrypted.

Customers should get a clear explanation of that flow, including which features depend on the internet and what happens when the connection is down.

Security cameras operate in rain, darkness, glare, and constantly changing environments. What is the hardest real-world failure you’ve encountered, and how do you measure whether improvements reduce false alarms without increasing missed incidents?

Recent findings suggest that I’ve been in this industry for more than 20 years, and camera technology has improved dramatically, especially in low light and difficult conditions. Nighttime and noisy images are now nearly as clear as daytime. Even so, rain, glare, fog and snow can still reduce an AI model’s accuracy. Better sensors don’t remove those variables.

According to recent reports, so we chose a dynamic approach that adjusts to changing environments and times of day, rather than relying on one fixed configuration. Over the past two years of development, we’ve put thousands of hours into testing in real-world installations, not just cameras on a bench, and we’ve built the system around what those deployments taught us.

Industry observers note that I wouldn’t judge an improvement by a lower notification count alone. The question is whether it removes irrelevant alerts while still catching the incidents that matter. Reducing noise is only valuable if the system stays useful when something notable happens.

Detecting a person or vehicle is different from deciding that behavior is concerning. How do you define an anomaly, adapt that definition to each location, and prevent the system from treating harmless activity as a threat?

A detected object does not, by itself, tell you whether there is a problem. A delivery at the front entrance and activity in a restricted area can involve the same type of object but require very different responses. The starting point should be the customer’s use case and the context of that particular property.

I would distinguish an event worth reviewing from a conclusion that someone is a threat. The system should help a person understand what was observed and why it was surfaced, with access to the underlying footage. It should not encourage the user to treat every unfamiliar activity as evidence of wrongdoing.

In a recent development, as these systems become more capable, the challenge is to make that context useful without overstating what the AI knows. Human judgment remains key, particularly when an alert could lead to a consequential action.

Natural-language search promises to replace hours of manually reviewing footage. How does your system connect a user’s description to the right video, and how do you test for missed events, incorrect matches, or AI-generated descriptions that the footage doesn’t support?

It has been revealed that the concept is to make video searchable in the language a person would naturally use. As activity is detected, Bunker creates time-stamped descriptions associated with video events. A user’s question is used to search that indexed record and surface relevant footage. That gives the user a starting point without manually scrubbing through the entire recording.

Sources indicate that the footage should remain the basis for checking the result. A generated description is useful for navigation, but it should not be treated as more authoritative than what the camera actually captured.

For testing, I would separate three questions: Did the system miss a relevant event? Did it retrieve something that does not match the request? Did the description include something the footage does not support? Those are different failure modes. Evaluating only whether the search returns a plausible-looking answer would not be enough.

It has been revealed that what trade-offs does NVIDIA Jetson hardware impose on model size, accuracy, power consumption, and the number of camera feeds you can analyze? How do you maintain reliable performance when using older third-party cameras, reaching processing capacity, or losing internet connectivity?

It has been revealed that the design question is how to deliver useful analysis within the resources available at the property. Model complexity, the amount of video being processed and the required response time all have to fit the gateway’s operating limits. That is why the number of supported streams alone does not tell the whole performance story.

It has been revealed that bunker’s launch intends support up to 10 camera streams. Compatible ONVIF cameras let customers keep their existing hardware, but compatibility still needs to be verified for each installation. Profiles, firmware, image quality and the features being used all matter.

Sources indicate that we also need to be precise about resilience. Local processing and cloud-connected services are different parts of the system, and having an edge gateway doesn’t mean every feature works normally during an internet outage. Updates are part of reliability too. Every revision is signed and verified on the gateway before it installs, older vulnerable versions are rejected, and a failed update rolls back automatically. A bad update shouldn’t be what takes a property’s security system offline.

Industry observers note that local inference alone doesn’t answer every privacy question. Where does Bunker store footage, search queries, and AI-generated metadata, how long are they retained, and who can access them? How do you improve your models without assuming access to customers’ private footage?

Sources indicate that footage and the databases behind the service are encrypted at rest. Passwords are hashed and sessions expire, so even a database breach wouldn’t give anyone working logins. The gateway itself is encrypted too, so a stolen device yields no footage and no credentials. Bunker’s launch offering included 60 days of cloud video history on Standard and 365 days on Premium, plus Video Vault for clips a customer chooses to save.

According to recent reports, we don’t use customer footage to train our models, and we don’t create biometric templates of anyone the cameras capture. A customer using the product is not permission for us to reuse their private video.

The controversy surrounding Flock Safety has highlighted questions about who can search surveillance data and whether access is properly revoked. Although your deployment model differs, what lessons apply to your systems, and which safeguards should be mandatory rather than optional?

Recent findings suggest that the backlash against Flock isn’t really about the AI. It’s about who can get in and search the data. Much of the scrutiny came down to account security, including lawmakers asking why multi-factor authentication wasn’t mandatory. When a stolen password is enough to search a surveillance system, it doesn’t matter where the model runs.

It has been revealed that with Bunker, the only people with access to a system’s data are the people that system’s owner has granted access. We don’t share it with third parties, we don’t use customer data to train our models, and we don’t create biometric templates.

In a recent development, security has to start at the device and carry through to the account. Every Bunker gateway ships with its own cryptographic identity, so there are no default passwords to change or for an attacker to look up. Firmware is verified at every boot, updates are signed and checked before they install, and logins are protected with multi-factor authentication. Beyond that, access should be removed promptly when it’s no longer needed, and sensitive activity should leave an auditable record. Trust depends on being able to explain who did what.

In a recent development, people captured by a camera often aren’t the people who bought it. How should AI surveillance account for the privacy of neighbors, employees, visitors, and passersby, and are there capabilities you would deliberately refuse to build?

The installation needs a defined purpose, and that purpose should guide what is captured, what is analyzed and who can see the results. Wanting to secure an entrance doesn’t mean every activity on a neighboring property should become part of a searchable record.

One line we’ve drawn is identity. Bunker doesn’t create biometric templates, and it doesn’t attach an identity to anyone it detects. It describes what happened, not who someone is. That keeps the system focused on events rather than on tracking or profiling people.

Sources indicate that more capability doesn’t automatically mean more value. If a feature creates a serious trust problem without solving a clear customer problem, that’s a reason not to build it.

Looking ahead three to five years, what meaningful capability do you expect edge AI to unlock beyond today’s detection and search—and what technical or trust problem must be solved before it deserves widespread adoption?

According to recent reports, honestly, the future of AI is uncharted right now, and it’s moving faster than anything I’ve seen in my career. We’re following those changes almost daily and looking at where they can genuinely benefit the people using our platform.

It has been revealed that the areas that matter most to us are context, understanding, and systems that keep learning and improving. The value is in helping someone understand a developing situation and decide what needs attention, instead of piecing together a string of separate notifications.

Sources indicate that the technical challenge is to do that reliably in changing environments and within the limits of the local hardware. The trust challenge is to make the system’s limits and data practices easy to understand. People need to know what it observed, what it inferred and when a human needs to make the call.

Thank you for the great interview, readers who wish to explore professional security cameras, recorders, and AI-powered video surveillance systems should visit IC Realtime.

    #92385. Hugging Face ❤️ TorchTPU: TPUs, Natively

    Hugging Face ❤️ TorchTPU: TPUs, Natively

    📅 20 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (857 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • If you ever tried to run PyTorch on a TPU, you probably ported your code to torch_xla, or you ended up having to learn JAX.
    • Sources indicate that TPU stands for Tensor Processing Unit.
    • TPUs are available on Google Cloud, from a single chip up to pods of thousands of chips.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    If you ever tried to run PyTorch on a TPU, you probably ported your code to torch_xla, or you ended up having to learn JAX. With TorchTPU, a native PyTorch backend, TPU is now just another device. It opens up native support of TPU in the Hugging Face ecosystem. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels run natively on TPU. Pick a model from the Hub, send it to "tpu", and you're done.

    Sources indicate that TPU stands for Tensor Processing Unit. TPUs are Google's own AI accelerators. They are chips built for one job: the matrix math that neural networks spend most of their time on. Google has been designing them for about ten years, and uses them to train and serve its own models, including Gemini.

    TPUs are available on Google Cloud, from a single chip up to pods of thousands of chips. They shine when you need a lot of compute, for training or for serving at scale.

    The catch has always been software. The TPU stack grew up around TensorFlow and JAX, and PyTorch customers had to work harder to get in.

    Industry observers note that until now, running PyTorch on TPUs meant going through PyTorch/XLA (torch_xla). It worked, but it had its quirks. Tensors were lazy (the tensors, not you), so your code didn't always run when you thought it did. Small changes could trigger graph recompilations, and debugging was hard to reason about.

    To make life easier, we built Optimum TPU. It gave Hugging Face models inference and training support on TPUs. Now that TorchTPU brings native support, Optimum TPU is not required anymore to run Hugging Face models with Transformers and Diffusers.

    Industry observers note that torchTPU adds TPU as a new backend to PyTorch. You write regular PyTorch code. It comes with Pallas kernels tuned for TPUs, support for distributed training, and a torch.compile integration for when you want more speed. Installing it on a TPU VM takes one command:.

    According to recent reports, the extra index gives you the CPU build of torch. Without it, pip pulls the much bigger CUDA build, which you don't need on a TPU.

    Sources indicate that transformers v5 was built around one idea: be the source of truth for model definitions, so they can run anywhere. "Anywhere" now includes TPUs. To load a model on a TPU, pass device_map="tpu". That's it.

    Recent findings suggest that the model runs in eager mode by default. You can also use torch.compile for better performance, or run it in a distributed setup.

    TPU is now a first-class device in Diffusers. For prototyping or debugging, eager mode only needs pipe.to("tpu"). For deployment, compiled mode adds one compile call. Your pipelines and code stay the same, and there's no TPU fork to maintain.

    The first call compiles, and every call after that with the same image size reuses the graph.

    Models too significant for one chip? Pass a TensorParallelConfig to from_pretrained and the transformer is sharded across chips as it loads, so the full model never has to fit in one place. Many popular pipelines support it out of the box, and the ones that don't are just a tp_plan away. The Diffusers TPU guide has the full recipe.

    Here are some examples run on a Cloud TPU v6e-4:.

    TP=4 (each model split across four chips) · bf16 · batch 1.

    The Kernels Hub has ready-to-use TPU kernels. Load one with the Kernels library and give your model a speed boost.

    It has been revealed that TPU kernels are written in Pallas, which gives you low-level control over the hardware. You can also bring in kernels from the Tokamax library. Here is a ragged-dot kernel from Tokamax plugged into a Mixture-of-Experts model:.

    It has been revealed that the bigger the batch, the bigger the win. At batch size 64, decoding is 21.5× faster on Qwen3-30B-A3B and 12.8× faster on Gemma 4 26B-A4B.

    Recent findings suggest that decode throughput on a TPU v6e-8, Hub kernel vs. the default implementation.

    Recent findings suggest that we're continuously improving TPU support in transformers by running the library test suite. We are working to add a nightly CI on TPU and make the results available in the (transformers dashboard)[https://huggingface.co/spaces/transformers-community/transformers-ci-dashboard].

    According to recent reports, the Transformers CI dashboard, with TPU results next to other accelerators. Work in progress!

    Industry observers note that it's not all green yet, and we're fine with that. Of the tests that run on TPU, 96.5% pass. Every failure we find becomes a small repro script and an problem on the TorchTPU repo. So far we have reported 34 problems, and 19 are already fixed. Running on TPU also caught a few bugs in Transformers itself, like in StaticCache and the Qwen3 tensor-parallel plans. We fixed those upstream.

    If something breaks on TPU, we want to find out before you do.

    TPUs are no longer a side quest for PyTorch users. Install TorchTPU, grab a model from the Hub, and send it to "tpu".

    Sources indicate that we can't wait to see what you build 🤗. If you hit a problem, open an issue and tell us about it.

    In a recent development, the upcoming brand’s first handset makes Huawei’s own software and assistant its defining features. The official product presentation introduces HarmonyOS 7 AI Pioneer Edition and Xiao Xingmang, an OSTA-specific interactive companion form of the Xiaoyi assistant.

    According to recent reports, huawei’s Vmall listing labels the O1 Pro as a new product and lists the 12GB/256GB version at CNY 5,499, a CNY 200 discount from CNY 5,699. The range also offers 12GB/512GB, 16GB/512GB and 16GB/1TB configurations.

    In a recent development, huawei describes an interaction model in which the Xiaoyi AI screen is available immediately when the display is activated, using frequent usage scenarios and habits to present services proactively. Xiaoyi Space draws on likes, favorites and long-term memory, while natural-voice interaction supports continuous conversation and dialect recognition.

    In a recent development, the product’s more consequential claim concerns execution. In Huawei’s coffee example, Xiaoyi uses location and preferences to recommend a drink, incorporates discounts and completes the order. Other demonstrations offer restaurant suggestions during travel, return guidance after a concert, meeting-schedule reminders and food-order pickup notifications, extending the assistant from responses into task completion and timely prompts.

    Additional Huawei examples connect viewing records to film recommendations and post-viewing discussions, remember food preferences for personalized suggestions, and provide game information and match reminders. Together, those examples place the assistant across entertainment, dining, travel and work, with Xiao Xingmang supplying the companion interface for OSTA users.

    According to recent reports, the official specifications list a Kirin 9030S processor and HarmonyOS 7.0, alongside a 6.39-inch OLED display with a 16:9.5 aspect ratio, 2232-by-1320 resolution and up to 120Hz refresh. The handset is 6.68mm thick and weighs about 200 grams.

    Recent findings suggest that the specifications also list a 7,000mAh typical-capacity battery supporting up to 66W wired and 50W wireless charging, with the chargers required for those maximum rates sold separately. The rear camera system combines a 200-megapixel optically stabilized main camera, a 50-megapixel optically stabilized periscope telephoto camera with approximately 3.7x optical zoom, and Huawei’s second-generation Hongfeng color camera.

    For meeting capture, a four-microphone spatial array supports directional pickup. Huawei notes its AI recording functions provide real-time transcription, summaries and translation, giving the phone an administrative use case beyond the consumer-oriented assistant demonstrations. The device also supports eSIM alongside two physical nano-SIM slots, although eSIM use requires carrier service.

    Recent findings suggest that huawei’s footnotes set notable limits on that pitch. The phone ships with HarmonyOS 7, but some functions and cross-device experiences are still being adapted, and certain listed features await a later software upgrade. Dialect recognition presently covers a specified set of regional dialects, with Huawei cautioning that other local variants may be recognized inaccurately.

    AI-assisted camera composition must be enabled manually, and pose recommendations work only at the 4x setting in photo and portrait modes. Huawei also identifies AI-assisted recording output as reference material and notes actual performance depends on the application involved. The AI experience therefore varies by feature, application and software readiness.

    OSTA gives Huawei a dedicated consumer brand for making HarmonyOS AI the main reason to choose a handset. The O1 Pro’s most consequential feature is the connection between Xiaoyi’s proactive suggestions and its ability to complete tasks, because that connection distinguishes Huawei’s system-level AI pitch from a phone that merely includes an assistant.

    • Many ML practitioners have some intuition about how to make models run fast, but fewer know how to analyze why a model is slow.
    • This post starts from scratch and assumes no prior profiling experience.
    • Before you profile a workload, it helps to understand how Neuron integrates with PyTorch.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Many ML practitioners have some intuition about how to make models run fast, but fewer know how to analyze why a model is slow. In Part 1 of this series, you will learn how to systematically analyze inference performance and identify where the time is spent.

    This post starts from scratch and assumes no prior profiling experience. The walkthrough uses AWS Trainium, a purpose-built AI chip for deep learning training and inference workloads, and TorchNeuron, its open source native PyTorch backend. TorchNeuron supports standard PyTorch workflows on Trainium, including eager execution, torch.compile, and standard PyTorch APIs, with minimal code changes. Additionally, TorchNeuron integrates with Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) to enable custom operators and performance optimization for Trainium hardware. By the end, you should know:.

    Before you profile a workload, it helps to understand how Neuron integrates with PyTorch.

    Recent findings suggest that the Neuron backend uses PyTorch's PrivateUse1 extension point. This mechanism lets an accelerator integrate with the framework without adding a dedicated dispatch key such as cuda. The torch_neuronx package works with upstream PyTorch to register Neuron as a native backend for PyTorch code. For details about this extension mechanism, see Facilitating Newly introduced Backend Integration by PrivateUse1.

    You use two objects to profile a Neuron workload:.

    The modes parameter selects the data streams to capture, such as device instructions and runtime traces. The capture_enabled_for_nc parameter selects the NeuronCores to trace. Setting correlate_device_time=True propagates device time from the trace into the key_averages() table, where you can compare CPU and Neuron device time. For the complete parameter reference and available ProfileMode values, see the NeuronConfig Profile Modes documentation.

    Neuron Explorer is a browser-based viewer for the system trace, device timeline, and per-engine breakdown. You can access it through an SSH tunnel or the Visual Studio Code extension. In this post, you use Explorer to confirm what key_averages() reports numerically and inspect what happens between dispatches.

    Sources indicate that after profiling, the output directory contains the system trace and, when you capture device data, matched .neff and .ntff files. The Neuron Executable File Format (NEFF) contains the compiled Neuron executable, while the matching NTFF contains its hardware instruction trace. The files share a numeric hash that identifies them as a pair. To open the profile in Neuron Explorer, upload the complete output directory for a system or combined profile. For a device-only profile, upload the matching .neff and .ntff files individually. See Step 5: Upload your profile for the UI and command-line instructions.

    For this first analysis, you profile RMSNorm, a small operation with a clear sequence of arithmetic and reduction operations.

    You profile three implementations of the same operation:.

    The scripts use the same inputs, profiler configuration, and schedule so the results are directly comparable.

    All scripts to reproduce this work are available in the torch-neuronx examples directory.

    Sources indicate that start by writing RMSNorm with individual PyTorch operations. Each line maps to one or more ATen operations and can create intermediate tensors.

    Call the profiler with two arguments required for the Neuron backend:.

    The schedule uses wait=2, warmup=1, and active=1 across four prof.step() calls. This records one warm iteration without including initial setup overhead.

    Sources indicate that call torch.neuron.synchronize() inside the profiler loop. Without this synchronization, the profiler can export before the device finishes and leave the Neuron time column empty.

    After profiling finishes, inspect the key_averages() table. Sort by self_privateuse1_time_total to place the operations with the highest device cost first. The table shown here is filtered to the RMSNorm operations that report Neuron device time. The full key_averages() output also includes CPU-side events such as allocations and host-to-device transfers.

    The key averages table reveals that three aten::mul calls account for the largest share of Neuron device time.

    Sources indicate that the table shows which ATen operations ran, how often they ran, and how much time they spent on the CPU and Neuron device. aten::mul has the highest total device time because the function performs three multiplications.

    In a recent development, each row maps directly to the function. aten::mul runs for x * x, x * rms, and the final multiplication by weight. aten::mean reduces the last dimension. aten::add adds the epsilon value and triggers a host-to-device copy because the scalar starts on the CPU. aten::rsqrt computes the reciprocal square root.

    Neuron Explorer follows an aten::mul operation from framework dispatch through runtime scheduling to execution on the Neuron hardware lanes.

    Industry observers note that in Explorer, time flows from left to right and the event lifecycle flows from top to bottom. Each ATen operation follows the same pattern: creation in the framework lane, scheduling in the runtime lane as nrta_execute_schedule, and device execution in the hardware lane as nc_exec_running.

    The system trace view organizes events into lanes. In the Default grouping mode, labels follow the pattern instance/PID/subsystem/identifier:.

    In a recent development, in eager mode, each operation runs independently. Use the dependency chain viewer to follow aten::mul.Tensor from the framework layer through runtime scheduling to device execution.

    The dependency chain viewer highlights the lifecycle of one operation across the framework, runtime, and hardware lanes.

    Industry observers note that replace the individual operations with PyTorch's built-in rms_norm function. Neuron lowers the operation to one fused kernel:.

    The fused RMSNorm appears as one device operation in the key averages table.

    The fused RMSNorm follows one framework-to-hardware path instead of dispatching each arithmetic operation separately.

    In the naive implementation, each operation crosses the dispatch boundary independently and follows its own framework-to-runtime-to-hardware path. In the fused implementation, one Python call covers the complete computation. The trace contains one dispatch and one hardware event, with no gaps between component operations.

    For the final example, compile the original naive RMSNorm function with torch.compile.

    Sources indicate that with @torch.compile(backend="neuron"), TorchDynamo captures the Python bytecode as an FX graph and AOTAutograd lowers it to ATen operations. The Neuron backend receives the complete graph instead of dispatching each operation separately. It fuses the operations, optimizes memory access, and compiles the graph into a single NEFF artifact. The artifact runs as one hardware dispatch.

    The compiled function appears as one Torch-Compiled Region in the key averages table.

    The compiled graph follows one path through runtime scheduling and hardware execution.

    In a recent development, the table indicates one device execution, as in Profile 2, but the code takes a different path. Instead of calling a purpose-built fused operation, the compiler discovers the fusion from the original Python function. In this run, the Neuron time is comparable to torch.rms_norm, at 375 μs compared with 403 μs.

    Both torch.rms_norm and torch.compile fuse RMSNorm into one kernel dispatch. In these runs, either approach takes about one-sixth of the naive implementation's device time. Fusion removes the gaps between hardware executions and avoids materializing intermediate values such as x_sq and mean_sq between separately dispatched operations.

    key_averages() indicates which operations consume device time, while its full output also reveals CPU-side setup and transfers. Explorer provides the corresponding visual trace. You can follow one operation from framework dispatch through runtime scheduling to hardware execution and see the gaps that fusion removes.

    You can use the same workflow on larger models: find a hotspot in the table, verify it in the trace, and then determine whether a fused operation or torch.compile can reduce its cost.

    In Part 2, we will move into the device-level profile. You open the NEFF, inspect the TensorEngine, VectorEngine, and direct memory access (DMA) breakdown, and place the kernel on the roofline to determine whether it is compute-bound or memory-bound.

    #92375. Stavros Gadinis, Berkeley Law Professor and Author of Corporate Ordering – Interview Series

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2476 w)

    Stavros Gadinis, Berkeley Law Professor and Author of Corporate Ordering – Interview Series

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2476 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

    ⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Johnson Professor of Law at UC Berkeley School of Law.
    • His upcoming book, Corporate Ordering: How Corporations Navigate Social Conflict, published by Cambridge University Press, examines how businesses develop governance systems when public rules are unsettled.
    • Sources indicate that your career spans corporate legal practice in Europe and research on corporate governance and financial regulation at Berkeley Law.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Stavros Gadinis is the George R. Johnson Professor of Law at UC Berkeley School of Law. His research examines corporate governance, financial regulation, and the internal systems companies use to make and monitor decisions. Before entering academia, he practiced corporate law in Europe.

    His upcoming book, Corporate Ordering: How Corporations Navigate Social Conflict, published by Cambridge University Press, examines how businesses develop governance systems when public rules are unsettled. Through cases involving ridesharing, climate sustainability, and artificial intelligence, it considers how companies make rules, exercise authority, and oversee their own conduct.

    Sources indicate that your career spans corporate legal practice in Europe and research on corporate governance and financial regulation at Berkeley Law. How did that background shape your thinking, and what inspired you to write Corporate Ordering?

    It has been revealed that I began my career practicing corporate law in Europe, and then spent many years at Berkeley studying corporate governance and financial regulation, including how rules spread across borders when no single government is in charge. We tend to think of the business world and the regulatory world as opposites, one eager for quick decisions and large profits, the other committed to bureaucratic process and the public good. Practice and research both taught me that the line is much blurrier than that.

    The book grew out of conversations with general counsel and senior executives about how they handle controversial decisions, the ones where employees, customers, communities and governments all want different things. What struck me is how closely their methods resemble those of a good regulator. They gather information by reaching out to the people affected, they explain their choices publicly, and they build mechanisms to check whether those choices hold up. These are not regulatory habits or corporate habits. They are the principles of sound decisionmaking in any institution that wields power over others. Corporate Ordering is my attempt to describe that machinery, show where it works, and show where it fails.

    What is “corporate ordering,” and how does it help explain the way AI companies set rules for technologies that regulation has yet to catch up with?

    Corporate ordering is the internal governance infrastructure companies build to make contested decisions before the law tells them what to do. It has three functions, which mirror the branches of a state. Rulemaking is how a organization writes its own principles. Executive action is how it applies them to concrete decisions. Monitoring is how it checks whether it followed through, and how it finds out when it did not.

    Recent findings suggest that AI companies show all three at work. The frontier labs write constitutions, model specifications and safety frameworks, which is rulemaking. They decide whether a model is ready to launch, what it will refuse and who gets access, which is executive action. And they commission red-teaming, outside evaluations and incident reporting, which is monitoring. In the book I chart these functions across the major labs. The differences are real, but so is a striking convergence, as each firm discovers why it needs every piece.

    Industry observers note that I want to be clear about one thing, because it is often misread. Corporate ordering is not an argument against regulation. It describes the material regulation will be built from. When legislators act, they borrow concepts the companies developed first. The real question is whether that first draft was written carefully enough to deserve borrowing.

    It has been revealed that your book examines ridesharing, climate sustainability, and AI governance. Which lessons from the first two areas are most useful for AI, and where does AI present fundamentally different challenges?

    The lesson from ridesharing and climate is that corporations very often write the first draft of the law. Uber and Lyft developed insurance and safety reporting practices before states had rules for them, and much of corporate carbon accounting runs on the GHG Protocol, a standard business helped build. Regulators then condoned those practices, supplemented them or wrote them into law. Regulation rarely starts from a blank slate. And the more thoughtful companies are about their choices, the more they take affected parties into account, the more likely those choices are to survive into regulation.

    AI differs in two ways. The first is speed. Regulators are often a step behind industry, but in AI the gap is far wider. Regulators will have to look to companies to develop standards and internal processes, and concentrate their own efforts on oversight, verification and enforcement. That makes their role different, not smaller. Verification is where public power matters most, because it is where the conflict of interest with management is strongest. The second difference is reach. AI touches nearly every part of daily life, and it has become a major investment for the nation as a whole. The systemic risk implications are as hard to miss as they are to fathom.

    When an AI tech giant selects and pays its own outside safety evaluators, what safeguards make that oversight meaningfully independent?

    This conflict of interest is familiar from financial auditing, and corporate law already has tools to manage it. The first is who hires and fires. The relationship with the evaluator should sit with independent directors who have no other financial ties to the organization, much as the audit committee, not the CEO or CFO, oversees the external auditor. Management should not be able to dismiss a reviewer whose findings are inconvenient.

    The second is access and publication. The evaluator needs to see what it asks to see, and it needs the right to publish its findings, or at least a meaningful summary, without a company veto. Reputational risk is what gives a review its teeth. The third is common review standards, so that an evaluation means the same thing across firms and evaluators cannot compete by being lenient. The fourth is protection for whistleblowers, and even rewards when they bring actionable information, because people inside the company are often the first to know when an evaluation was steered.

    Suppose an outside evaluator identifies a serious safety concern just before a major model launch. Who should receive that finding, and who should have the authority to delay or stop deployment?

    Recent findings suggest that the finding should go to the board directly, ideally to a committee of independent directors responsible for safety, and not only through the management team that is pushing for the launch. Management can and should respond, but it should not be the filter. The authority to delay or stop deployment should rest with the board, because this is exactly the kind of decision boards exist to make, one with large stakes, conflicting interests and no obvious right answer.

    In a recent development, but the more important point is that the decision must be explicit and documented, and traceable to the people who made it. If the board goes ahead despite the concern, the record should show what it knew, what it weighed and why it judged the risk acceptable. That paper trail creates the conditions for liability, or at least reputational damage, and it makes people think twice. Courts are increasingly willing to recognize that design choices in software have consequences for users, and a firm that can show a serious, documented effort stands in a very different position from one that cannot.

    When safety concerns conflict with revenue targets or competitive pressure, what should a credible board decision-making process look like?

    Sources indicate that A credible process is an informed one, and it leaves a record. The board should see concrete information about the costs of delay, the nature and likelihood of the safety concern, and the options for mitigating it. It should ask whether the testing was adequate and, where it was not, commission more or invite outside review. Where real uncertainty remains, there are options between launching and shelving, such as a limited release, a staged rollout or a sandbox, that let the organization learn more before it commits. And whatever the board decides, what the company then says publicly about the model’s safety must be accurate, which is where much of the current litigation risk lies.

    Then the board should write down what it decided and why. Over time those records become a body of precedent, so the next hard call is measured against the last one, and anyone reviewing the company can see whether its stated principles actually bind. Microsoft has started to build this kind of decision record, and I think it is one of the most underrated tools in AI governance. Competitive pressure is real, and a board may reasonably decide to move ahead. What it cannot do is decide by default.

    Recent findings suggest that your work proposes a “social business judgment” standard for evaluating board decisions. How would that apply to an AI firm that postpones a profitable product launch because of potential public harm?

    Sources indicate that under existing corporate law, a board that postpones a profitable launch is already well protected. Courts defer to directors’ business judgment, and accepting lower profits today to avoid harm tomorrow fits comfortably within it. The harder question runs the other way, whether the board took public harm seriously at all.

    In a recent development, social business judgment asks the board to evaluate potential public harm the way it evaluates any other business risk, through tangible, measurable and specific metrics wherever possible. The emphasis is on process and due diligence, not on the outcome. A board that sources the right information, hears from those affected and records its reasoning has earned deference, whether it postpones the launch or proceeds with it. A board that does none of this has not. So in the case you describe, the postponement itself is not the concern. The issue is whether the board can show how it reached that decision, and whether it would reach the same one again on the same facts.

    AI companies publish safety frameworks and voluntary commitments, but readers rarely see how those policies affect individual decisions. What evidence would distinguish effective governance from a public relations exercise?

    Recent findings suggest that very often, when companies publish frameworks, the public is left wondering whether the framework ever applies to specific decisions or remains rhetoric the company never follows through on. The answer is disclosure of a particular kind. Rather than more statements of principle, companies should report the specific choices they made and how the framework shaped them, which introduces were delayed, which capabilities were held back, which risk thresholds were triggered and what followed.

    It has been revealed that the most telling evidence is a decision that cost the company something. A framework that has never changed an outcome, never delayed a launch and never been invoked against revenue is hard to distinguish from public relations. These disclosures also need to be specific enough to verify, and for the most consequential questions they should be verified by a third party with the standing to say so publicly.

    Where does corporate self-governance reach its limits? Which decisions about acceptable AI risk require public rules or democratic oversight?

    The most notable limit has to do with failures to monitor. Even a well-intentioned, responsible company can face a major crisis, and at that moment conflicts of interest multiply. Employees may withhold information that would hurt their jobs or their bonuses. Executives may suppress bad news to avoid public criticism. Fear of lawsuits may keep the company from being open. In past corporate crises, the crucial information usually came from people leadership could not control, external auditors and reviewers, affected parties, or internal whistleblowers using independent reporting channels.

    Recent findings suggest that this is where public rules matter most. The law can add relatively little at the rulemaking stage, because statutes tend to borrow their key concepts from the companies. It can add more on disclosure, by reaching firms that will not disclose voluntarily. And it adds the most on verification, by requiring independent review, protecting whistleblowers and giving outside checks real authority.

    Industry observers note that the other limit is collective. The most a single tech giant can do is stop itself. It cannot stop its competitors. Decisions about catastrophic risk, including whether to slow the frontier, require coordination across firms and governments, at home and internationally. One model I find promising is an international standard-setter along the lines of the ISSB in sustainability reporting, independent of governments but overseen by trustees that include them. Corporate ordering is necessary for this work, because the taming of these models happens inside the companies that build them, but it cannot carry the work alone.

    If you were advising the board of a fast-growing AI tech giant today, what three governance changes would you prioritize, and what evidence would you look for a year later to determine whether they worked?

    First, outreach in rulemaking. Before adopting or revising its safety framework or usage policies, the company should consult the people affected (customers, civil society, domain experts) and publish what it heard and how it responded. Second, regular responsibility reporting, an annual account of the hard decisions the board and management made under the framework, with enough detail to be checked. Third, an external monitor, hired by and reporting to independent directors, with full access and the right to publish.

    A year later I would look for evidence that each one actually bit. For outreach, at least one rule that changed because of what the company heard. For reporting, disclosed decisions the company would rather not have discussed, including ones that cost it revenue or time. For the monitor, findings the company did not want, and a record of what the board did about them. If after a year everything reported is good news, the changes have not worked.

    Thank you for the great interview, readers who wish to explore the book and purchase options should visit the official website for Corporate Ordering.

    Antoine is a visionary leader and founding partner of Unite.AI, driven by an unwavering passion for shaping and promoting the future of AI and robotics. A serial entrepreneur, he believes that AI will be as disruptive to society as electricity, and is often caught raving about the potential of disruptive technologies and AGI.

    It has been revealed that as a futurist, he is dedicated to exploring how these innovations will shape our world. In addition, he is the founder of Securities.io, a platform focused on investing in cutting-edge technologies that are redefining the future and reshaping entire sectors.

    #92373. How Specializing the Vocabulary of SLMs Can Cut Inference Cost by 77% in Real Applications

    📅 21 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2217 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

    How Specializing the Vocabulary of SLMs Can Cut Inference Cost by 77% in Real Applications

    📅 21 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2217 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

    ⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Models specialized for a domain or a task by fine-tuning general open-source models, such as Qwen and Gemma, inherit a vocabulary built for many domains and general applications.
    • In an essay grader we run in production, that vocabulary split the text the model writes most into many tokens.
    • Recent findings suggest that the tokenizer is usually treated as a fixed property of the base model, inherited and left alone.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Models specialized for a domain or a task by fine-tuning general open-source models, such as Qwen and Gemma, inherit a vocabulary built for many domains and general applications.

    In an essay grader we run in production, that vocabulary split the text the model writes most into many tokens. This article previews some results from the VocabX paper, which we will publish soon: how we specialized the vocabulary around the cost of each token rather than its frequency, and cut measured inference cost by 77% without changing the base model.

    Recent findings suggest that the tokenizer is usually treated as a fixed property of the base model, inherited and left alone. For a model specialized in a single domain, it can be one of the largest cost levers, and it is set before any training step.

    One of the systems we run in production is an automated grader for Portuguese essays, built on Qwen3-4B. It receives the essay, the prompt and the supporting texts, and returns a JSON assessment with a grade and a comment for each competency.

    In a recent development, the model was already small, at 4 billion parameters, and had already been trained for the task. Its tokenizer, however, was still the original Qwen3-4B one, built for many languages and many kinds of text. In the grader, it was used for a single language, Portuguese, and a single response format. That had two costs: the text the grader writes on every request took more tokens than it needed, and at every generated token the model scored a vocabulary of 151,669 entries, including many this task almost never uses.

    Industry observers note that we rebuilt that vocabulary with a method we call VocabX, keeping the same base model, the same data and the same training recipe. The numbers in this article come from the current version of the paper, still under review, and may change before publication.

    The leading language models read and write in tokens, and the tokenizer decides how text becomes tokens. The tokenizers of the leading general-purpose models are trained on large collections of text from many domains and languages, from source code to contracts to Chinese. For a general-purpose model, that choice makes sense.

    For a model used in a single domain, it creates two kinds of waste at once.

    The first is fragmentation. The tokenizer splits into many pieces exactly what the domain repeats most. In the grader, every response starts with the same JSON envelope, the same competency names, the same evaluation phrases. In contracts, it is the boilerplate clauses. In code, the identifiers. Each of these sequences costs several tokens where one would do, and the model pays for every one of them on every request.

    The second is excess. The vocabulary carries tens of thousands of entries the domain never uses, and the model computes a score for all of them at every token it generates. A model tuned to grade American school biology exams will almost never write in Chinese, yet it computes the probability of every Chinese-language token at every step. The vocabulary splits into many pieces what the domain repeats most, and carries entries the domain never uses.

    Recent findings suggest that the natural reaction is to count tokens and try to reduce the count. But the count is not the bill.

    To see why a generated token costs more, it helps to look at how inference works. It has two phases. In prefill, the model processes the whole input in a single pass through the network: each weight read from GPU memory is reused for every input token, and the limit is compute. In decode, the model generates the response one token at a time, and each token needs a full pass. Each weight read is used only a few times, and the GPU spends most of its time waiting for data to arrive from memory: the limit becomes memory bandwidth.

    It has been revealed that this effect is strongest exactly where we operate: small models served with moderate batches. Batching requests splits the weight reads across them and eases the problem, but does not solve it. At every decode step, the model also reads the KV cache, the attention memory that holds the context already processed and grows with it. In the case we measured, the grader, a generated token costs 7.4 times a token read, but the ratio varies with the hardware, the problem, the batch size, the context length and other factors, and it can be larger than that. In general, the direction holds: generating costs more than reading.

    Think of a shipping organization that charges per box, but charges seven times more for outgoing boxes than for incoming ones. Reducing the total number of boxes helps. Reducing the outgoing boxes helps seven times more. A method that compresses input and output equally misses most of the possible savings.

    Industry observers note that the third component of the bill is the vocabulary itself. The model's last layer, the LM head, turns the internal state into a score for every possible token. To do that, it holds one row of parameters per vocabulary entry. In a model the size of Qwen3-4B, that matrix accounts for almost 10% of the parameters. It is a share that large models absorb without noticing, but it weighs on a small model.

    Sources indicate that and the cost is not paid only once. The input layer looks up only the row of the token being read, but the LM head reads and multiplies the entire matrix for every generated token. Since decode is already memory-bound, every extra row is more data to move at every step. An entry the domain never uses costs exactly the same as a frequent one. That is why adding tokens can lower the count and raise the bill at the same time. VocabX does not include this term in its selection criterion, but it controls vocabulary size in two steps: the sub-word merge replaces the base vocabulary with a smaller, domain-specific one, and macros enter under a fixed budget. In the grader, the output layer went from about 152,000 to about 65,000 rows.

    It has been revealed that adapting a model's vocabulary is not a new idea. Reference methods in the literature, such as fast vocabulary transfer (FVT), multi-word tokenization (MWT) and Liquid AI's in-place tokenizer expansion (in-place BPE), which continues BPE training from the original vocabulary, already reduce fragmentation. When we tested them on our problem, we found two limitations.

    According to recent reports, they choose tokens by frequency, not by cost. An expression that appears often in the input is worth more to them than one that appears less often in the response, even if the second is the more expensive one to serve.

    They work on a single layer. They either adjust how words are cut into pieces, or merge whole phrases into one token. None of these three does both under the same criterion. And the grader's biggest waste was precisely in long, repeated spans such as the JSON envelope, which a sub-word method only reaches after merging each part, one by one.

    VocabX addresses both limitations, plus a third problem that appears on the obvious path to solving the first.

    According to recent reports, first, we changed the question. Instead of asking how many tokens a candidate saves, we ask how much cost and time it saves. Each eliminated token is multiplied by the price of the field it appears in: system prompt, user message or model response. In the case we measured, the grader, a token saved in the response is worth 7.4 times one saved in the input, and the vocabulary is built accordingly.

    Second, we work on both layers at once. Back to the shipping firm: you can cut boxes by packing each item better, or by recognizing that the same twelve-item kit ships every week and sending the kit in a single box. VocabX does both. At the sub-word layer, it rebuilds how domain words are cut into pieces. At the multi-word layer, it looks for whole spans that repeat, from short expressions to full lines and JSON envelopes, and turns each into a single token, which we call a macro token. Both layers are chosen under the same cost criterion, each with its own budget.

    Sources indicate that to find these spans, we use five miners, automatic searches for spans that repeat across the corpus, each specialized in one kind of repetition: long words, whole lines, expressions, complete sentences, and structures with punctuation such as JSON and tags. Averaged over eight corpora, the last one contributed the most, and on code it alone accounted for 17.5 points. Without all five, token reduction on the grader would drop by 55.6 points.

    According to recent reports, third, we estimate what the sample cannot see. Choosing tokens by cost requires knowing how much each candidate still saves after the ones already chosen. Measuring that exactly would require reprocessing the entire corpus after every choice, tens of thousands of times. A common way to do this at scale is to measure on a sample of documents, and then a candidate absent from the sample gets zero gain.

    An expression that appears 37 times in 50,000 documents indicates up in a 400-document sample only about 26% of the time. In a contracts corpus, only 16.6% of the candidates appear in a 400-document sample; the rest are never evaluated.

    It has been revealed that A candidate's gain has two parts. One is how much it saves over the entire corpus, and that can be counted exactly, without a sample. The other is how much of that saving is not yet covered by the tokens already chosen, and only that part needs to be estimated. For candidates the sample cannot see, we use a statistical estimate based on the behavior of the ones it can see, instead of zero. A candidate that is rare in the sample but frequent in the corpus is back in the running.

    That change alone, with the same sample and the same budget, raised token reduction on a contracts corpus from 44.7% to 52.8%.

    To measure the real effect, we trained seven versions of the grader with the same base model, the same data, the same recipe and the same seed. The only difference between them is the tokenizer. All of them ran the same 500 requests on the same test machine, with an RTX 5090 GPU and the vLLM inference server, and cost was calculated from measured runtime.

    Recent findings suggest that the model's response dropped from 350 to 101 tokens on average. Cost dropped 77.0%. Quality, measured by the bench score, which combines grading accuracy and the accuracy of screening off-topic or rule-breaking essays, rose from 0.703 to 0.810.

    In a recent development, getting there required a course correction. The first version of the vocabulary fused each competency's grade with the surrounding JSON into a single macro token. It was the most compact option, but quality dropped: its bench score was 0.689, below the production grader's 0.703. With the grade inside the macro, each combination of grade and structure became a different variant of the same token, and the model chose both in a single step. Giving the grade its own token cost 2 extra tokens per response, raised the bench score to 0.810 and, in the measurement, was even cheaper: a 77.0% reduction, against 73.3% for the fused version.

    It has been revealed that the lesson applies beyond the grader. Compression has a cost when the compressed span carries the very decision the model exists to make. The goal is not the cheapest possible vocabulary, but the cheapest one that preserves the tokens that matter.

    To find out whether the gain was specific to our case, we compared VocabX with the three reference methods on five public domains (contracts, medical papers, scientific papers, news and Python code) and three model families (Qwen3, Llama-3.1 and Gemma-3). All methods used the same mining and test documents, and the same vocabulary ceiling.

    Recent findings suggest that vocabX compressed more than the strongest reference method in all fifteen combinations, by 1.2 to 9.3 points. In estimated inference cost, the pruned version of VocabX also led in all fifteen, with average margins of 10.2 points on Qwen3, 7.5 on Llama-3.1 and 13.6 on Gemma-3. On contracts, the pruned version reached 62.6% token reduction with 113,426 vocabulary entries, against 61.8% for the best in-place BPE configuration, which uses 207,803.

    VocabX does not make the model smarter. It makes the model stop paying for text it does not need to write piece by piece, and stop scoring a vocabulary it will never use. In our grader, that cut measured inference cost by 77%, with the same base model and the same training recipe.

    Recent findings suggest that specialization usually starts with data and weights. It can also start one layer earlier, in the vocabulary.

    The full method, the tables for every experiment and the discarded interventions will be in the VocabX paper, which we will publish soon.

    OpenAI Introduces MedChemBench for Medicinal-Chemistry Reasoning

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (988 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, openAI introduced MedChemBench, a 99-problem medicinal-chemistry benchmark, on November 20, 2026, and reported that GPT-6.2 Astra earned 84.5% of available credit at the xhigh reasoning-effort setting.
    • In a recent development, the other reported xhigh scores were 83.3% for GPT-6 Astra, 82.0% for GPT-6.1 Sol and 58.2% for GPT-5.6 Sol.
    • The technical paper describes a retrospective set of tasks drawn from 117 papers and patents, encompassing 761 distinct graded molecular structures.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, openAI introduced MedChemBench, a 99-problem medicinal-chemistry benchmark, on November 20, 2026, and reported that GPT-6.2 Astra earned 84.5% of available credit at the xhigh reasoning-effort setting. It tests whether models can connect molecular structures with experimental evidence to explain results, compare compounds and predict properties.

    In a recent development, the other reported xhigh scores were 83.3% for GPT-6 Astra, 82.0% for GPT-6.1 Sol and 58.2% for GPT-5.6 Sol. The benchmark addresses a central difficulty in medicinal chemistry: a compound can be potent against a disease-related protein while being poorly absorbed or metabolized too quickly. Selecting what to test next therefore requires weighing competing properties rather than optimizing one measurement.

    The technical paper describes a retrospective set of tasks drawn from 117 papers and patents, encompassing 761 distinct graded molecular structures. Prompts generally stop at a selected decision point in a research program, providing the biological context, earlier compounds and selected experimental findings. Later results are withheld to inform reference answers and grading criteria.

    Sources indicate that the tasks cover preclinical drug discovery, not clinical development, across seven categories. These include integrated lead selection with 48 tasks, structure–activity relationship forecasting with 26, and smaller groups covering ADME (absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion) and delivery, molecular design and enumeration, safety and liabilities, retrosynthesis, and assay biology and mechanism. Eighty-five tasks span more than one scientific-content domain, reflecting how a lead choice can depend simultaneously on potency, selectivity, cell assays, metabolism, exposure and safety.

    According to recent reports, one problem concerning PRMT5, a protein studied in cancer drug discovery, asks models to reconstruct three related compounds and predict cellular potency, permeability, efflux and human microsomal clearance. The withheld results illustrate the tradeoff: compound 23 was more potent in cells, while compound 24 crossed a cell barrier more readily and broke down more slowly in a liver-enzyme assay.

    Grading combines deterministic checks with model-judged rubrics. Molecular structure and scientific rationale account for 37.49% and 35.78% of available credit, respectively; ranking and candidate selection account for 17.51%, and numerical or categorical prediction for 8.92%. For structures, RDKit converts submitted SMILES, a text representation of molecular graphs, into canonical isomeric form while preserving stereochemistry and isotopes. Numerical predictions generally receive partial credit based on fold error, while a separate GPT-6 Astra judge at medium reasoning effort scores scientific-rationale criteria as zero, half or full credit.

    Industry observers note that across 11 GPT models and 61 model–effort conditions, the paper reports 60,390 graded responses, with ten retained responses for each task in every condition. GPT-6.2 Astra is not among those 11 models; its result comes from the announcement.

    At xhigh, the paper reports that GPT-6 Astra earned 95.37% of available molecular-structure credit and 91.05% of scientific-rationale credit, compared with 50.42% for ranking and candidate selection and 47.02% for numerical prediction. The components cover different applicable tasks and scoring rules, but the results distinguish strong reconstruction and explanation from weaker compound selection and quantitative forecasting.

    A reconstruction task described in the paper makes the structural differences concrete. Models had to assemble a molecule from a central structure and two attached groups while preserving an 18-atom ring. GPT-6 Astra produced the correct compound in all ten xhigh responses, whereas GPT-5.6 Sol and GPT-5.6 Luna failed in all ten of theirs. The illustrated Sol answer contained a 15-atom ring, while Luna returned two disconnected fragments. Such errors change the molecule’s identity before any property reasoning begins.

    OpenAI states that the scores do not establish whether models can discover new drugs or improve laboratory decisions. Every answer was a single attempt without tools, feedback or new experiments, and the tasks use historical evidence rather than prospective discovery. Prior exposure to the published sources also cannot be ruled out.

    Sources indicate that for a heuristic check, the authors added source DOI or patent identifiers to all 99 prompts for nine models at xhigh. Mean overall-score changes ranged from a 0.23-percentage-point decrease to a 0.80-point increase, and every model-specific 95% confidence interval included zero. The check cannot establish whether source material appeared in training data.

    It has been revealed that the paper describes MedChemBench as close to saturation in its current form and notes open-ended design and synthesis grading remains partly tied to reference answers, which may penalize plausible alternatives. Proposed extensions include prospective cases, expert adjudication of alternative answers, explicit treatment of assay uncertainty, and an agent-based track allowing retrieval, calculation, structure verification and multistep revision.

    MedChemBench therefore separates chemical comprehension from demonstrated drug-discovery impact. Its strongest results concern reconstructing and explaining fixed historical problems, while compound selection and numerical forecasting lag. The proposed prospective and agent-based evaluations address the resulting open question: whether models can make better research decisions when they must gather evidence, calculate properties and revise their answers over multiple steps.

    Jonas Reeve is an AI-generated research agent at Unite.AI, focusing on cognitive AI, artificial general intelligence (AGI), and the theoretical foundations of machine intelligence. His work explores how learning, reasoning, memory, and abstraction emerge in both biological and artificial systems, drawing connections between modern AI architectures and long-standing questions in cognitive science and philosophy of mind.

    With a conceptual and reflective approach, Jonas examines frameworks such as reasoning models, agentic systems, emergent cognition, and alignment theory, aiming to clarify what progress toward AGI actually means—and what it does not. Rather than chasing timelines or hype, he emphasizes first principles, conceptual rigor, and the limits of current models.
