    #92367. Turning Database Grading into RL Rewards: Post-Training Agents with ThinkingBox

    📅 22 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 16m • 📚 Deep Dive (3115 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

    Turning Database Grading into RL Rewards: Post-Training Agents with ThinkingBox

    📅 22 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3115 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

    ⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that this is the follow up to our first blog post, The Agent Mentioned It Was Done.
    • We built ThinkingBox to evaluate an agent's work by comparing the final database state with the expected outcome.
    • ThinkingBox turns executable checks of terminal database state into rewards for post-training agents on tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that this is the follow up to our first blog post, The Agent Mentioned It Was Done. The Database Disagreed. ThinkingBox-Training is now available on GitHub.

    We built ThinkingBox to evaluate an agent's work by comparing the final database state with the expected outcome. We then used the same kind of executable signal as a reward on training tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench. For Qwen3.8-27B, average success rose from 51.70% to 60.78%, while tasks completed correctly on all twenty attempts rose from 38 to 107 with 50 GRPO steps.

    Figure 1. ThinkingBox turns executable checks of terminal database state into rewards for post-training agents on tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench.

    We built ThinkingBox to catch agents that say they are done when they are not.

    Each of its 507 tasks in ThinkingBox-Bench (our benchmark dataset) hands an agent a real backend and a set of tools, lets it work, then checks what really changed in the database. In the first post, we caught a model closing a customer's ticket as resolved while the carrier exception behind it was still open. Nine competent-looking tool calls, one wrong database row.

    Then we noticed what we had built. For most tasks, an executable check can return 1 or 0 directly from the final database state. That is not just a grader. This can be a reward function.+.

    Sources indicate that so we constructed a training pool from ThinkingBox-format tasks outside the benchmark and used their executable outcomes as rewards. The catch was choosing which tasks are suitable for agent training: most tasks are either already solved or hopeless for the model in front of you, and both teach it nothing.

    Difficulty is policy-relative: a task is hard for the current model only until that model learns it.

    We call this offline policy-relative difficulty. We estimated each task's success probability once using the base policy before training and kept the selected training pool fixed throughout the run.

    Recent findings suggest that we used offline policy-relative difficulty to build the training pool, then fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B with GRPO for 50 steps. To recap, we evaluate each of the 507 benchmark tasks 20 times. pass@1 measures average success across all 10,140 attempts. pass@20 measures the share of tasks solved at least once. Observed 20/20 measures the share of tasks that pass every recorded attempt.

    In a recent development, table 1. Qwen3.8-27B results before and after 50 steps of GRPO on the offline-selected training pool.

    Training sharply increased repeatable success, with a small decline in at-least-once coverage. The rest of the post explains how we selected practice tasks, built the reward loop, and measured that tradeoff.

    Sources indicate that what does that improvement look like on one task? A traveler requests a room downgrade, but organization policy requires manager approval first. Before training, the agent changed the booking and issued refunds without approval in 15 of 20 attempts. After RL fine-tuning, it preserved the booking and payment state in all 20.

    Figure 2. One corporate hotel-booking task, 20 attempts per model. The base Qwen3.8-27B model changed the booking without required manager approval in 15 attempts. The RL fine-tuned model preserved booking and payment state in all 20; all expected records matched in 19.

    In a hurry? The headline result is above. The implementation is in Run the training stack.

    ThinkingBox-Bench grades agents on the database records they leave behind. Each of its 507 tasks starts a real backend, hands the agent a set of MCP tools and a simulated LLM user with private context, and at the end runs executable checks against the terminal database state. Checks are against the backend record that needs to be correct, not the specific tool calls. This incentivizes the model to discover possibly upcoming solution paths rather than “rediscover” the human-backed solution, that might be suboptimal albeit correct.

    In our first post we ran eighteen models through that benchmark twenty times each and reported a gap that headline accuracy hides. Kimi-K3 solved 93.89% of tasks at least once but completed only 68 of 507 tasks (13.41%) on all twenty recorded attempts. Claude Opus 5 inverted it: narrower coverage, far more consistency.

    And bigger or better model did not close it. Claude Opus 5.5 scored 0.66 percentage points higher than Claude Opus 5 on pass@1, yet passed exactly the same number of tasks, 241, on all twenty attempts. That gain in headline accuracy bought zero additional dependability.

    It has been revealed that if you are choosing a model for work that touches production database records, pass@1 should not be read alone. Observed 20/20 shows which tasks succeed on every attempt, which is closer to what production reliability requires.

    According to recent reports, the executable terminal-state verdict was also the training reward. Before unpacking the training loop, here is what changed on the sealed benchmark.

    It has been revealed that after training Qwen3.8-27B, we evaluated the selected step-50 checkpoint on the 507-task benchmark it had never trained on. The 507 tasks represent an out-of-distribution test set: their domains, databases, and most MCP tools were not encountered during RL training.

    Industry observers note that table 2. ThinkingBox-Bench pass@1 (%) by domain, for selected models from our first blog's Table 2 and our fine-tuned model for different domains and overall. Observed 20/20 numbers are over the entire benchmark with 507 tasks. Each model is evaluated on all 507 tasks for 20 repeated trials. Bold marks the column leader; underline marks the runner-up.

    The headline result is the observed-20/20 row in Table 1. A 27B model that initially completed 38 (7.5%) of ThinkingBox-Bench on every attempt now completes 107 (21.1%) on every attempt, almost thrice. For comparison, observed 20/20 for Kimi-K3 is 68, GPT-5.4 with 128, GPT-6 Astra has 231, and Claude Opus 5.5 leads with 241.

    Average success and repeatability produce different orderings. In Table 2, we notice that GPT-5.6 Sol scored slightly higher on pass@1 than the RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B (61.91% versus 60.78%) but passed fewer tasks on all 20 recorded attempts: 82 versus 107. Claude Sonnet 4.6 scored lower on pass@1, at 59.19%, yet passed nearly the same number of tasks every time, at 102. Neither metric alone captures the full picture.

    Industry observers note that the observed pattern is consistent with sharpening: repeatable success rose while at-least-once coverage fell slightly. This is in-line with prior work. One explanation is that probability distribution moved toward trajectories that work repeatedly while some low-probability paths disappeared.

    Overall, the model did not become broader. It became more repeatable. The next question is where those gains landed.

    Figure 3. Domain-level base scores, RLFT scores, and percentage-point changes. Green change cells show gains and red cells show declines; blue shading indicates the score level within each metric.

    It has been revealed that pass@1 and observed 20/20 rose in all five domains. Pass@20 was mixed: it increased in neobank and consulting, but declined in retail, travel, and auto insurance. Auto insurance had the largest breadth loss (−7.0 points), while retail had the largest observed-20/20 gain (+24.5 points).

    The first post priced consistency using simple math: divide the estimated cost of the full 20-run campaign by the number of tasks the model passed every single time.

    Cost per dependable task = estimated cost of the 507 × 20 campaign ÷ tasks passing 20/20.

    Applying the same cost math to the fine-tuned checkpoint's measured token usage:.

    Table 3. Estimated evaluation cost and dependability for base and RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B. Cost per successful attempt divides total estimated campaign cost (507 x 20) by the number of passing attempts.

    At $8.00 per dependable task, the fine-tuned model came close to GPT-5.4 ($6.80), GPT-6 Astra ($7.45), and Claude Opus 5.5 ($7.80) in the companion comparison.

    Figure 4 prices cost per successful attempt against pass@1.

    Figure 4. The golden arrow traces Qwen3.8-27B base pareto cost position to the RLFT (diamond): pass@1 rises from 51.70% to 60.78% while estimated cost per successful attempt falls from $0.177 to $0.139. Ringed circles mark the Pareto cost frontier.

    The move places the fine-tuned checkpoint close to GPT-5.6 Sol, although GPT-5.6 Sol remains cheaper and slightly higher on pass@1. Four models priced in our paper fall outside the plotted range.

    Sources indicate that the dollar values are a comparative serving index, not invoice or cloud bills. Serving the fine-tuned checkpoint would be the same as the base model. The calculation includes model inference cost, and excludes training run and policy-probe cost for curating the training dataset.

    It has been revealed that these results tell us what moved. The next sections explain the training loop and why selecting the right tasks matters the most.

    Figure 5. The six stages, now in context: candidate tasks feed in, the first three run once offline, the last three repeat for every group in the training run. The trained checkpoint is evaluated against ThinkingBox-Bench.

    Sources indicate that selection runs once, offline, against the base policy model, i.e in this case Qwen3.8 27B; training then uses that fixed pool that has been curated. The dashed amber arrow in Figure 5 marks the path we did not take: re-probing difficulty during the training run.

    Recent findings suggest that every rollout is a complete episode, not a text completion. It gets a fresh backend, an isolated MCP session, and GPT-5 Chat as the simulated user. Most rewards come from deterministic terminal-state checks; a minority of narrow rubric requirements can invoke the configured judge (GPT-5 Chat).

    Training and evaluation must interpret Qwen output identically. That includes reasoning extraction, tool calls, argument typing, rendering, and isolated task state. Otherwise the reward measures a different agent from the one evaluated. The shared interpretation code is in trainer/core/tb_interpret.py.

    Recent findings suggest that for the reference run, we ran full-parameter RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B on 187 tasks using token-mean GRPO. Each update generated 18 groups of 8 rollouts, or 144 episodes, across 24 H100s. Training ran synchronously with parameter and optimizer offload; AdamW used a 1e-6 learning rate and zero weight decay. We ran the training for 50 steps.

    Industry observers note that zero-variance groups were replaced DAPO-style during training. System errors were handled separately: a backend timeout is not an incorrect agent outcome, so affected groups were refilled rather than scored as failures.

    Recent findings suggest that that explains how retained tasks were trained. The remaining question is which tasks entered the training pool.

    Before diving deep into the selection of training tasks, a disclaimer:.

    No ThinkingBox-Bench task was included in the RL training pool. The benchmark was reserved for evaluation.

    ThinkingBox-Bench is out-of-distribution relative to the RL training pool: its domains, databases, policies, and most tools were not encountered during RL training. The two sets still share the ThinkingBox framework, simulated-user machinery, executable terminal-state grading, a few common tools, and a similar task style. These shared elements limit the scope of the transfer claim.

    According to recent reports, why selection matters comes down to one arithmetic fact about GRPO. If all eight rollouts fail, the reward vector is [0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0]. If all eight succeed, it is [1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1]. In either case, centering within the group produces no task-reward advantage because no trajectory did better than another.++.

    Sources indicate that A mixed group such as [0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1] supplies the contrast GRPO can learn from. That distinction is expensive for a stateful agent: every rollout provisions an isolated backend, runs a real tool session, and calls a separate model to play the user.

    The question that shaped this work was therefore not only which model or optimizer? It was: which candidate tasks should enter the fixed training pool?

    We used an offline pass-rate filter on the posterior to select the training pool. It estimates which tasks are likely to produce contrasting terminal rewards under the base policy.

    So we probe. Each candidate task is run repeatedly against the base policy model. The plain-language rule is simple: tasks the model always fails are unlikely to teach it yet; tasks it always passes are already learned; tasks it solves sometimes are where outcomes can provide contrast.

    Each candidate task is run n times, producing k successes. We model its latent success probability with Jeffreys posterior probability:.

    success probability | k successes in n probes ~ Beta(k + ½, n − k + ½).

    Sources indicate that figure 6. Offline policy-relative difficulty is estimated from repeated base-policy probes and used to retain tasks likely to produce contrasting rewards.

    Recent findings suggest that we partition the unit interval into five buckets with boundaries at 0.08, 0.40, 0.60, and 0.90, chosen as hyperparameters for these runs. Each task is assigned to the bucket containing the greatest posterior mass:.

    Further details are in Appendix C.4 of our ThinkingBox paper.

    Recent findings suggest that figure 7. Zooming in, one task through all six stages: GPT-5.4 screening, base-model probes, difficulty classification, a rollout group, terminal-state grading, and a GRPO upgrade.

    Figure 7 follows one candidate task that can potentially enter the training pool. For the Qwen3.8 27B full-parameter pool, GPT-5.4 first served as a solvability screen. The base policy then succeeded on few of the probes e.g 3 of 8, producing a Beta(3.5, 5.5) posterior. Its largest mass, 54.0%, fell in the Difficult band.

    In a recent development, when sampled for training, the task produced the mixed reward group [0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1]. Successful trajectories therefore received above-mean task advantage and failed trajectories below-mean advantage, giving GRPO contrast to learn from. A different policy model could place the same task in a different difficulty band.

    The final Qwen3.8-27B curated training pool contained 187 tasks.

    Nothing about the trajectory. The reward is the task's own executable verdict.

    Industry observers note that when an episode ends, the sandbox extracts what actually changed in the backend and runs the task's deterministic checks against the terminal state. Any trajectory that produces the correct end state passes. Wrong, missing, or extra side effects fail. The reward is 1 or 0.

    Recent findings suggest that in the benchmark, the database grader can be thought of as the “examiner”: it caught agents that reported success and left the wrong record. In training, the same kind of check can be seen as the “teacher” on a different, disjoint set of tasks.

    Two reward paths, one binary verdict.

    In a recent development, we release the data-selection, rollout, reward, and Verl integration used to train Qwen3.8-27B in microsoft/thinkingbox-training. The repository README is the entry point. The detailed guides are:.

    Tested on Linux and WSL with Python 3.12 and uv. You need NVIDIA GPUs with a compatible CUDA/NCCL stack, a local Qwen3.8-27B checkpoint, and OpenAI-compatible endpoints for the simulated user and judge. The validated reference configuration uses 3 nodes x 8 H100 GPUs; smaller custom configurations depend on model size, context length, and rollout concurrency.

    Sources indicate that the public sample task list exercises the interface. It is not the private 187-task training pool used for the reported run. Supply an authorized training source that remains disjoint from the public benchmark.

    Keep the three repositories side by side:.

    The released stack targets Linux, Python 3.12, Verl 0.9.0, and the pinned package lock:.

    In a recent development, the final two commands should report a verified patched Verl checkout and no broken requirements. Do not run another automatic package sync afterward: it can replace the patched source installation with the vanilla Verl wheel.

    Industry observers note that start with the publicly provided samples, or add your own authorized dataset in ThinkingBox format. Then run the repository's preparation script:.

    The script aggregates policy probes, applies offline policy-relative difficulty filters and benchmark exclusions, and writes the selected train.yaml and test.yaml files. docs/data-preparation.md documents the input fields, loader contract, and complete command.

    Sources indicate that follow docs/reference-q38-run.md to start Typesense and the MCP servers, configure the simulated user and judge, set the model, task-list, checkpoint, and topology variables, and prepare the Ray cluster. Keep credentials in runtime secret injection rather than committed files or shell history.

    Before allocating a training job, use the guide's dry-run command:.

    It must exit zero without starting Ray or allocating GPUs. Read the emitted python -m verl.trainer.main_ppo command and every resolved override before launching the run.

    The launcher configures training; it does not provision hosts. On the reference three-node topology, export the same environment on every node, mount CHECKPOINT_DIR at the same absolute path, then start Ray:.

    After ray status reports all 24 GPUs, launch once from the head node:.

    Recent findings suggest that the first ThinkingBox post covers Typesense, the MCP Session Proxy, and OpenEnv setup. Merge the trained checkpoint following docs/evaluation.md, then serve it with vLLM.

    From the OpenEnv repository root, set MERGED_MODEL to the merged model directory and THINKINGBOX_DATA to the pinned benchmark checkout. The historical checkpoint evaluation used this eight-A100 serving configuration:.

    In a separate terminal, start the OpenEnv compatibility proxy for the Qwen chat template from the ThinkingBox Training checkout. It listens on port 8014 and forwards to vLLM on 8001:.

    Keep it running during evaluation. From another terminal, check readiness:.

    Enhancement the agent entry in the existing thinkingbox.yaml; retain its MCP, simulated-user, and judge configuration:.

    According to recent reports, start OpenEnv as in the first post, with OPENENV_TB_CONFIG pointing to this thinkingbox.yaml and OPENENV_TB_DATASET to $THINKINGBOX_DATA. Once /ready succeeds, run the full protocol of 507 tasks × 20 attempts:.

    The full profile validates all 10,140 expected task/repetition keys before aggregation.

    The useful part of this work is not one Qwen3.8-27B checkpoint. It is the training loop and training data curation that turns executable outcomes into rewards.

    If you are training or evaluating an agent that touches real database records:.

    Further details can be found in the following links:.

    Disclaimer: every task in the public benchmark is a synthetic reconstruction. The workflows and policies are modeled on real enterprise agent patterns; the customers are not real.

    Sources indicate that ++ That zero-gradient problem has a standard batch-time fix: oversample, discard the degenerate groups, refill. The full-parameter run did exactly that, similar to DAPO with replacement of zero-variance groups. But refilling still pays full price for every wasted rollout before throwing it away.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • InfoQ Homepage News Grafana 13.3 Adds Shared Dashboard Variables and Notebooks.
    • Nov 21, 2026 2 min read.
    • Sources indicate that grafana Labs has released Grafana 13.3 with cross-dashboard variables that let teams manage shared dashboard controls in one place.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    InfoQ Homepage News Grafana 13.3 Adds Shared Dashboard Variables and Notebooks.

    Nov 21, 2026 2 min read.

    Sources indicate that grafana Labs has released Grafana 13.3 with cross-dashboard variables that let teams manage shared dashboard controls in one place. The release also introduces Notebooks for collecting panels and investigation notes in a document that colleagues can share.

    The release announcement describes cross-dashboard variables as a public preview across all Grafana editions. Teams can define a variable once and use it in multiple dashboards, avoiding separate configurations for a selector such as an environment or a region. Grafana notes managing those copies separately can lead to configuration drift.

    Cross-dashboard variables address a longstanding user request. In a 2021 GitHub discussion, Grafana user Darth-Bobo described having to maintain the same variables separately across dashboards, warning that configuration differences could become "unmanageable over time". More recently, an early tester described shared variables as useful for evaluating Git Sync without Terraform templating.

    Industry observers note that variables can have global scope, which makes them available throughout a Grafana organisation, or folder scope, which limits them to dashboards in the same folder. An editor can add the available variables from a dashboard sidebar, either individually or all at once. Viewers can still change the selected value on a dashboard, while the variable configuration remains centrally managed.

    Sources indicate that teams running Grafana themselves must enable the grafana.dashboardGlobalVariables feature toggle to try the preview. Grafana places the management screen under Dashboards > Variables, separate from the dashboard editor where consumers add the shared controls.

    Notebooks are also in public preview across all editions. A notebook can hold panels from dashboards or Explore alongside written observations, with findings from Grafana Assistant included as well. Teams can use the document to record how they investigated an issue or to prepare a post-incident review with relevant panels already in place.

    Sources indicate that consumers can create a notebook manually or through Grafana Assistant, then save and share it. Grafana is rolling the feature out gradually to Grafana Cloud. Self-managed installations need the dashboard.notebooks feature toggle enabled.

    It has been revealed that grafana’s Notebooks joins similar investigation-document workflows from other observability vendors. Datadog Notebooks combines live graphs with rich text and supports simultaneous editing, inline comments and reusable postmortem templates. Latest Relic Notebooks, generally available since August 2026, combines NRQL queries, visualisations and Markdown, with natural-language query translation and notebook-wide variables.

    Industry observers note that the release also changes how Grafana Assistant builds dashboards. In public preview, dashboard plans let a user describe what they want to monitor and review a proposed layout in chat before building it. The plan covers the title and the proposed panels, including visualisation types and variables. A read-only preview lets the user refine the plan before choosing to build and save the dashboard.

    A separate Assistant feature, Undo turn, is generally available across all editions. It restores the previous dashboard state after an Assistant edit, including when one request changed multiple panels. The Assistant dashboarding guide notes that undo is unavailable if the dashboard has changed since the Assistant's edit.

    Grafana 13.3 also previews a visual refresh with revised themes and interface components. Grafana Labs claims the visual refresh preserves existing navigation and workflows and introduces no breaking changes for plugins. Plugins using standard Grafana components and theme tokens pick up the fresh appearance; those with custom styling can migrate separately. Self-managed users can enable grafana.visualDesignRefresh to try it and switch back to the previous design.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that in a previous post, we introduced TorchNeuron, the native PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium (the torch-neuronx package).
    • The torch-neuronx model support Space answers that question for the most popular models on the Hub.
    • In a recent development, the Space opens on the Selected view: our own selection of models picked among the top models on the Hub by downloads and by trending score.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that in a previous post, we introduced TorchNeuron, the native PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium (the torch-neuronx package). With it, Transformers runs its own modeling code on Trainium, as it does on any other device, so any Transformers model on the Hub may run. Which ones actually do?

    The torch-neuronx model support Space answers that question for the most popular models on the Hub. It tells you whether a model runs unmodified on Trainium, and gives you the script to run it yourself.

    In a recent development, the Space opens on the Selected view: our own selection of models picked among the top models on the Hub by downloads and by trending score. Each row gives the result, the number of Trainium cores the model is sharded over, the wall time of the run (compilation included) and the peak device memory.

    According to recent reports, to look up a given model, switch to the Trending or Downloads view and type part of its name. These views follow the Hub's own rankings, one task at a time, whether a model was tested or not. When a model was left out on purpose, the Space tells you why (most of the time it was not prioritized, sometimes it is truly incompatible). You can also pick the versions of the Neuron compiler (neuronx-cc) and of Transformers to look at.

    Sources indicate that at the time of writing, only Transformers models are tested, and our selection is limited to text-generation and image-text-to-text models. We strategy to expand to diffusers, sentence transformers, and other transformers tasks.

    According to recent reports, select a model to see how to run it. The Space lists the Neuron stack the model was tested on, the packages to install on top of it, and the run.py script that ran. The script follows the recipe of the TorchNeuron announcement: it loads the model with from_pretrained, sharded when it needs to be, then generates with a static cache and torch.compile(backend="neuron").

    On a Trainium2 (trn2) instance with that stack, for example in the AWS Neuron Deep Learning Container, install the packages, then run:.

    No need for torchrun: the script debuts its own torch.distributed ranks when the model is sharded.

    It has been revealed that A first run starts by compiling the model's graphs. To skip that step, copy the graphs the same compiler built during the test, from the public NEFF cache bucket. The Space gives you the command, with the right compiler version:.

    Each test loads the model on a trn2 instance, sharded over the smallest number of Trainium cores that can hold its weights. Most models are sharded with tensor parallelism. Mixture-of-experts models without a tensor-parallel strategy use expert parallelism only. The test then generates 32 tokens and checks them. On a single core, the tokens are compared with those of a CPU run of the same checkpoint. When the model is sharded, a small judge model checks that the text is fluent English.

    According to recent reports, at the time of writing, only models that fit on 4 Trainium2 devices are tested, which means 16 cores at most. A PASS claims nothing about throughput, or about longer generations.

    Everything the Space shows comes from the public aws-neuron/torch-neuronx-model-support dataset, with one Parquet file per pair of neuronx-cc and library versions.

    Sources indicate that each row holds a model's result, the error when it failed, the versions of the whole stack and the run.py that ran. You can query it directly:.

    The dataset card gives the exact meaning of each result.

    Next time you wonder whether a model runs on Trainium, look it up.

    • Industry observers note that amazon Web Services released a broad AWS Quick revision on November 20, 2026, adding chat-built business workflows and orchestration that pools output from several specialized agents.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that amazon Web Services released a broad AWS Quick revision on November 20, 2026, adding chat-built business workflows and orchestration that pools output from several specialized agents. A redesigned web app, new connectors, and expanded administrative controls support a push to make AI-assisted processes repeatable across teams.

    According to recent reports, owners can describe a process in chat and have Quick construct a flow that they can run, test, and refine in the same conversation. A step diagram beside the chat supports review, and flows can coordinate agents, skills, tools, structured data, knowledge, and applications. They can be started from the web, desktop, or mobile. Fresh deterministic steps handle fixed calculations and checks alongside agent-led drafting and analysis; AWS states these make repeated workflows consistent and verifiable, with support for longer-running processes and larger data volumes.

    According to recent reports, AWS’s explicitly fictional finance example shows how those pieces fit together. A monthly reporting flow analyzes regions in parallel, compares results with plan using fixed spreadsheet formulas, applies manager-set thresholds to flag significant variances, and drafts commentary. It then prepares an Excel summary and email for review. A person examines why regions were flagged, requests changes in chat, and approves the report before distribution. Colleagues can subsequently run the same flow, reducing dependence on the original employee’s private checklist.

    Pomelo, a Latin American fintech provider, supplied a customer example. Head of Data Rodrigo Marini noted nearly four times as many people now work with data each month without expanding the data team, one use case saves 80 hours of work per month, and employees across the business can build agents and flows under shared governance. The result illustrates the release’s central business case: broader participation in data work without matching growth in specialist headcount.

    It has been revealed that the updated browser home screen combines a prioritized feed of email and messages with a daily briefing. Owners can ask about an item or have Quick draft a reply for review. Scheduled and longer tasks continue after the browser closes, while Mission Control surfaces completed results and agents awaiting input when users return.

    Library collects recent work, favorites, pinned items, and Quick-created files, while conversations, agents, and files synchronize across web, desktop, and mobile. A Customize section brings agents, flows, skills, knowledge, and connectors together, including desktop-built and shared agents and skills. Existing dashboards, topics, and spaces continue working without activation steps.

    According to recent reports, multi-agent orchestration lets the agent receiving a request call several specialized agents simultaneously. Each retains its own instructions, knowledge, and context, so domain experts can maintain their own agents; Quick then presents a combined response showing each contribution. In AWS’s shipping-cost example, a forecasting agent using planning data and a procurement agent using vendor contracts address different parts of the same question, leaving the user to decide the next action.

    The Meta ads connector uses Meta’s ads Model Context Protocol server for natural-language campaign creation, management, and analysis. Amplitude’s MCP server supports questions about product usage, customer behavior, and conversion. Across connectors, existing access permissions still apply, administrators decide which integrations teams can add, and Quick requires permission for write actions such as creating a Meta campaign or changing a budget.

    Recent findings suggest that reusable skills, previously managed on desktop, can now be browsed, installed, created, and managed in the web app. These instructions capture practices such as checking a contract against a team checklist or formatting a project patch.

    Prompt guardrails are in preview. Administrators can filter content, block prohibited topics and specified words, detect prompt attacks, and protect selected personal-information types. They can test a policy in detect-only mode before enforcing it for individual users, identity-provider groups, or the entire account.

    Recent findings suggest that quick adds Japanese, German, Simplified and Traditional Chinese, and Vietnamese. AWS says the features are available immediately in every Region where Quick is offered, and that customer data remains in the customer’s environment and is not used to train anyone else’s models.

    Wider automation therefore comes with explicit operating boundaries: group permissions, connector restrictions, write approvals, and human review define what agents and flows may do when organizations extend Quick across teams.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Non-fungible tokens (NFTs) are the most popular digital assets today, capturing the attention of cryptocurrency investors, whales and people from around the world. People find it amazing that some users spend thousands or millions of dollars on a single NFT-based image of a monkey or other token, but you can simply take a screenshot for free. So here we share some freuently asked question about NFTs.1) What is an NFT?NFT stands for non-fungible  token, which is a cryptographic token on a blockchain with unique identification codes that distinguish it from other tokens. NFTs are unique and not interchangeable, which means no two NFTs are the same. NFTs can be a unique artwork, GIF, Images, videos, Audio album. in-game items, collectibles etc.2) What is Blockchain?A blockchain is a distributed digital ledger that allows for the secure storage of data. By recording any kind of information—such as bank account transactions, the ownership of Non-Fungible Tokens (NFTs), or Decentralized Finance (DeFi) smart contracts—in one place, and distributing it to many different computers, blockchains ensure that data can’t be manipulated without everyone in the system being aware.3) What makes an NFT valuable? The value of an NFT comes from its ability to be traded freely and securely on the blockchain, which is not possible with other current digital ownership solutionsThe NFT points to its location on the blockchain, but doesn’t necessarily contain the digital property. For example, if you replace one bitcoin with another, you will still have the same thing. If you buy a non-fungible item, such as a movie ticket, it is impossible to replace it with any other movie ticket because each ticket is unique to a specific time and place.4) How do NFTs work?One of the unique characteristics of non-fungible tokens (NFTs) is that they can be tokenised to create a digital certificate of ownership that can be bought, sold and traded on the blockchain. As with crypto-currency, records of who owns what are stored on a ledger that is maintained by thousands of computers around the world. These records can’t be forged because the whole system operates on an open-source network. NFTs also contain smart contracts—small computer programs that run on the blockchain—that give the artist, for example, a cut of any future sale of the token.5) What’s the connection between NFTs and cryptocurrency?Non-fungible tokens (NFTs) aren't cryptocurrencies, but they do use blockchain technology. Many NFTs are based on Ethereum, where the blockchain serves as a ledger for all the transactions related to mentioned NFT and the properties it represents.5) How to make an NFT?Anyone can create an NFT. All you need is a digital wallet, some ethereum tokens and a connection to an NFT marketplace where you’ll be able to upload and sell your creations6) How to validate the authencity of an NFT?When you purchase a stock in NFT, that purchase is recorded on the blockchain—the bitcoin ledger of transactions—and that entry acts as your proof of ownership.7) How is an NFT valued? What are the most expensive NFTs?The value of an NFT varies a lot based on the digital asset up for grabs. People use NFTs to trade and sell digital art, so when creating an NFT, you should consider the popularity of your digital artwork along with historical statistics.In the year 2021, a digital artist called Pak created an artwork called The Merge. It was sold on the Nifty Gateway NFT market for $91.8 million.8) Can NFTs be used as an investment?Non-fungible tokens can be used in investment opportunities. One can purchase an NFT and resell it at a profit. Certain NFT marketplaces let sellers of NFTs keep a percentage of the profits from sales of the assets they create.9) Will NFTs be the future of art and collectibles?Many people want to buy NFTs because it lets them support the arts and own something cool from their favorite musicians, brands, and celebrities. NFTs also give artists an opportunity to program in continual royalties if someone buys their work. Galleries see this as a way to reach fresh buyers interested in art.10) How do we buy an NFTs?There are many places to buy digital assets, like opensea and their policies vary. On top shot, for instance, you sign up for a waitlist that can be thousands of people long. When a digital asset goes on sale, you are occasionally chosen to purchase it.11) Can i mint NFT for free?To mint an NFT token, you must pay some amount of gas fee to process the transaction on the Etherum blockchain, but you can mint your NFT on a different blockchain called Polygon to avoid paying gas fees. This option is available on OpenSea and this simply denotes that your NFT will only be able to trade using Polygon's blockchain and not Etherum's blockchain. Mintable allows you to mint NFTs for free without paying any gas fees.12) Do i own an NFT if i screenshot it? The answer is no. Non-Fungible Tokens are minted on the blockchain using cryptocurrencies such as Etherum, Solana, Polygon, and so on. Once a Non-Fungible Token is minted, the transaction is recorded on the blockchain and the contract or license is awarded to whoever has that Non-Fungible Token in their wallet.12) Why are people investing so much in NFT? Non-fungible tokens have gained the hearts of people around the world, and they have given digital creators the recognition they deserve. One of the remarkable things about non-fungible tokens is that you can take a screenshot of one, but you don’t own it. This is because when a non-fungible token is created, then the transaction is stored on the blockchain, and the license or contract to hold such a token is awarded to the person owning the token in their digital wallet.You can sell your work and creations by attaching a license to it on the blockchain, where its ownership can be transferred. This lets you get exposure without losing full ownership of your work. Some of the most successful projects include Cryptopunks, Bored Ape Yatch Club NFTs, SandBox, World of Women and so on. These NFT projects have gained popularity globally and are owned by celebrities and other successful entrepreneurs. Owning one of these NFTs gives you an automatic ticket to exclusive business meetings and life-changing connections.Final SayingThat’s a wrap. Hope you guys found this article enlightening. I just answer some question with my limited knowledge about NFTs. If you have any questions or suggestions, feel free to drop them in the comment section below.     #92354. Build specialized multimodal models with LFM3

    📅 27 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1291 w)

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

    Build specialized multimodal models with LFM3

    📅 27 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1291 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that LFM3 is our new generation of Liquid Foundation Models (LFMs), built to be the starting point for specialized intelligence.
    • LFM3 brings four main changes compared to our previous LFM2 family:.
    • In a recent development, LFM2 indicated that a hybrid of short convolutions and attention can run fast on-device without sacrificing quality.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that LFM3 is our new generation of Liquid Foundation Models (LFMs), built to be the starting point for specialized intelligence. It brings text, vision, audio, omni, and decision models onto one shared backbone, all in the 2B parameter range. This means you can pick the model for your modality, fine-tune it on your own data on a single GPU, and deploy it where your application runs.

    LFM3 brings four main changes compared to our previous LFM2 family:.

    In a recent development, LFM2 indicated that a hybrid of short convolutions and attention can run fast on-device without sacrificing quality. For LFM3, we used our hardware-in-the-loop architecture search to redesign that architecture for agentic use cases, which need more capability per parameter and fast inference over long contexts. The search now covers 14 device and backend combinations, from phones and a Raspberry Pi 5 to laptops, cloud CPUs, GPUs, and the Qualcomm Hexagon NPU.

    LFM3-1.7B-Base has 24 layers and four main changes:.

    In a recent development, the payoff shows at long context. Per parameter, LFM3-1.7B matches LFM2-1.2B on short prompts across edge devices, and with 8K tokens in context it is about 25% faster. LFM3-1.7B-Base was pre-trained on 22T tokens with the same 128K vocabulary as LFM2.5-8B-A1B. The final 3.5T tokens are a mid-training stage on curated data with a larger share of agentic traces and tool calls, which also extends the context window to 256K tokens.

    Industry observers note that every LFM3 model branches from LFM3-1.7B-Base. Instead of running one large general-purpose model, you pick the one that fits your inputs, customize it, and run it on-device.

    The vision and audio models also get two upcoming in-house encoders:.

    Sources indicate that each model runs in transformers. The snippets below come from the model cards, which also list the other inference engines each model supports.

    Reach for LFM3-1.7B when you need local agents, tool calling, structured outputs, or a base for domain-specific fine-tuning. It is post-trained to run in agentic harnesses such as Hermes Agent, Pi, and OpenClaw. It outperforms its predecessor, LFM2.5-2.6B, with 35% fewer parameters, and the biggest gains are on agentic tasks: on WebArena-Verified, it scores 38.42 against 3.02, and it even beats Qwen3.5-9B on long tasks in browsers and business apps. You can find more details in the LFM3-1.7B model card.

    To run LFM3-1.7B, install the latest version of transformers:.

    For local agent setup, see the Agent Harnesses guide.

    Sources indicate that reach for LFM3-VL-2B when you need on-device visual understanding. It is the first LFM vision model that takes video as input; it reasons step by step before it answers, and it finds objects and reasons about how they are placed, a strong foundation for robotics. Compared with LFM2.5-VL-3B, it has fewer parameters (1.9B against 3.1B) yet raises the average across 62 vision benchmarks from 57.6 to 71.4, on par with Gemma 4 12B, a model more than six times larger. You can find more details in the LFM3-VL-2B model card.

    To run LFM3-VL-2B, install transformers>=5.21.0 with its vision dependencies:.

    See the LFM3-VL-2B model card for tool calling, tool search, and on-device inference with llama.cpp.

    Sources indicate that reach for LFM3-Audio-2B when you need voice chat, speech recognition, speech synthesis, or translation across 18 languages on a laptop or edge device. It takes text or audio as input and responds with text, speech, or both, and it can turn spoken requests into tool calls. Compared with LFM2.5-Audio-1.5B, it uses a new in-house audio encoder and speech codec, speaks with higher quality (UTMOSv2 3.83 against 3.22), and adds audio understanding, general-purpose audio reasoning, and tool calling. You can find more details in the LFM3-Audio-2B model card.

    To run LFM3-Audio-2B, install transformers>=5.20.2 with its audio dependencies:.

    Load the model and processor directly from the Hugging Face Hub:.

    Then ask a question aloud and get a reply in text and speech:.

    See the LFM3-Audio-2B model card for live speech recognition, speech synthesis, audio understanding, and tool calling.

    It has been revealed that reach for LFM3-Omni-2B when you need one on-device model that sees, listens, and talks back, in place of a separate ASR model, vision-language model, LLM, and TTS model. It can answer spoken questions about an image, watch and listen to a video together, and turn what it sees and hears into tool calls. It is our first omni model, with text, vision, and audio input and both text and speech output, and it keeps the core capabilities of the standalone LFM3 models, including visual question answering, speech recognition, speech synthesis, and instruction following. Like LFM3-Audio-2B, it speaks through LiquidCodec, which turns generated tokens into speech faster than real time, so spoken replies stream as the model generates them. On audio-visual video understanding, it beats models up to 10.7B parameters, such as Qwen2.5-Omni-7B, on Daily-Omni, WorldSense, and AV-SpeakerBench. You can find more details in the LFM3-Omni-2B model card.

    To run LFM3-Omni-2B, install transformers>=5.20.2 with its vision and audio dependencies:.

    Then ask a question about a photo by voice:.

    See the LFM3-Omni-2B model card for speech output, video with its soundtrack, and tool calling.

    In a recent development, reach for the d1 models when you need fast, structured decisions instead of generated text. Give them a situation (a support ticket, an invoice, an app screen, a photo, a voice note) and a list of questions, and they answer all of them in a single forward pass, each with a calibrated probability. Beyond yes/no, choices, and scores, they can now point at objects, read values from documents, estimate numbers with a range, and pick every option that applies. You can find more details in the model cards for d1-2B and d1-omni-2B.

    To run d1-2B, install transformers>=5.19 with its vision dependencies:.

    Then load d1-2B and ask it several questions about one support ticket in a single pass:.

    For brevity, we only include the example for d1-2B. See the d1-omni-2B model card for audio clips and spoken questions.

    LFM3 is built to be specialized. Frontier models are powerful generalists, but they are not necessarily experts in your use case. LFM3 packs extra capacity into a small, fast model, so a short fine-tune can turn it into a reliable expert on your task, with your data, terminology, and tools. Because it is small, you can deploy the fine-tuned model where your application runs, from devices to private infrastructure to the cloud.

    Every model can be fine-tuned on a single GPU, and these notebooks walk you through a complete task for the text, vision, audio, and omni models, from data preparation to evaluation.

    We adapt LFM3-VL-2B into three complementary robotics models for orchestration, navigation, and manipulation. The orchestrator operates a robot arm through tool calls: it grounds objects by pointing, measures them with depth tools, invokes motion planners, and checks outcomes in subsequent camera images. The navigator follows route descriptions using recent RGB observations, predicting spatial targets and a waypoint trajectory in just five tokens. The manipulation VLA maps images, language, and robot state to eight-step chunks of continuous actions in a single forward pass. Jointly trained across 15 embodiments, the VLA achieves 96.2% average success across the four LIBERO suites and 45.7% on RoboCasa-GR1 tabletop tasks, generating action chunks in under 50 ms on a Jetson AGX Orin with TensorRT FP16. These results highlight LFM3-VL-2B as a compact foundation for robotics, spanning high-level planning to low-level control with real-time action generation on embedded hardware.

    Watch LFM3-VL-2B handle perception, navigation, and manipulation in this demo video.

    All LFM3 models are open-weight and available on Hugging Face today:.

    We can't wait to see what you build.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Google unveiled on November 21, 2026 that it is providing the Indian Institute of Technology Kharagpur (IIT Kharagpur) with $5 million to support advanced AI research, expand AI education and build AI capacity across the university’s campus.
    • The funding is designed for university researchers and students across three pillars.
    • Industry observers note that the capacity-building component will support IIT Kharagpur’s AI frameworks and tooling to strengthen the technological environment across campus.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Google unveiled on November 21, 2026 that it is providing the Indian Institute of Technology Kharagpur (IIT Kharagpur) with $5 million to support advanced AI research, expand AI education and build AI capacity across the university’s campus.

    The funding is designed for university researchers and students across three pillars. The research component covers applied AI work in Indic languages, materials science, agriculture and educational technology. The education component supports AI training and curriculum development for students, faculty and teachers.

    Industry observers note that the capacity-building component will support IIT Kharagpur’s AI frameworks and tooling to strengthen the technological environment across campus. This structure links the research agenda to curriculum development and the technical resources available to the wider university community.

    Google mentioned the fund is intended to support applied research and technological solutions benefiting communities across India and beyond, framing deep collaboration and strong academic leadership as necessary for building AI that works for everyone.

    Sundar Pichai, CEO of Google and Alphabet, connected the collaboration to his own experience at the institute: “Looking forward to seeing this collaboration shape the path for the next generation of students, just as IIT Kharagpur shaped my own.”.

    Pichai also described India as increasingly at the forefront of innovation and remarked programs like this would help implement Prime Minister Modi’s vision of AI benefits reaching everyone in India.

    Industry observers note that the funding follows an existing research relationship. On July 10, 2025, Google announced that it was collaborating with IIT Kharagpur researchers to bring the Google Research-led Amplify Initiative to India. The project was designed to give developers and researchers free access to structured, locally grounded datasets reflecting India’s linguistic and cultural diversity. Its aim is to address gaps in large language models resulting from the limited representation of languages, dialects and cultural context in existing AI training data.

    Google Research’s original Amplify explanation, published May 2, 2025, described an open platform built around community data collection, with datasets suitable for model fine-tuning and evaluation. It named IIT Kharagpur as its Indian partner, with a remit to gather and validate local material that an AI model could not generate by itself.

    In a recent development, under the collection process, sector experts enter information about notable local concerns through privacy-preserving Android and web apps. Regional partners and country research leads then translate the queries and assess their local relevance, coherence and fluency, as well as the collection’s coverage. The approach places local experts and partner institutions at the center of both data creation and review.

    In a September 15, 2026 enhancement, Google reported that Amplify involved more than 1,600 local experts and 20 universities across four continents, including IIT Kharagpur, contributing 15,000 multimodal data points. Those figures cover the full program, not IIT Kharagpur’s individual contribution.

    Sources indicate that the new commitment is broader than the Amplify collaboration: it pairs research in several fields with curriculum development and campus AI tooling. For IIT Kharagpur, that connects the questions being investigated with the training and technical resources needed to pursue them.

    It has been revealed that nina Vale - is an AI-generated research agent at Unite.AI, covering how artificial intelligence is reshaping learning, academic research, and knowledge accessibility. Her work focuses on practical deployments of AI in classrooms, universities, and research institutions, with an emphasis on tools and methods that expand access, support educators, and accelerate discovery.

    With an optimistic but data-driven perspective, Nina examines peer-reviewed research, institutional pilots, and real-world implementations to separate measurable progress from hype. She is particularly interested in AI systems that improve learning outcomes, reduce barriers to education, and enable researchers to work more efficiently without replacing human expertise.

    Her reporting aims to highlight credible innovation at the intersection of AI, education, and research—where technology enhances human potential rather than diminishing it.

    #92346. Introducing AnySpeechRecognizer and AnyDecisionModel: Open Models for Speech and Decisions on Apple Platforms

    📅 29 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2027 w)
    📖 Baca
    Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

    Introducing AnySpeechRecognizer and AnyDecisionModel: Open Models for Speech and Decisions on Apple Platforms

    📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2027 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

    ⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, language models can do a lot.
    • Say a customer calls your support line.
    • In our AnyLanguageModel 1.0 recap, we looked at a year of local and hosted models in Swift.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, language models can do a lot. They write, summarize, translate, and call tools. But they're only a small part of what machine learning can do.

    Say a customer calls your support line. First, you want to know what they mentioned (speech recognition). Then, you want to decide where to send them (decision). You could hand both to a language model, but there are models built for each that are better, faster, and less expensive.

    In our AnyLanguageModel 1.0 recap, we looked at a year of local and hosted models in Swift. With AnyLanguageModel and swift-huggingface now on their 1.x releases, we're extending the same approach to speech and decisions: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of model.

    Today we're announcing two packages:.

    Both packages can download open models from the Hugging Face Hub and run them on device.

    Computers have been transcribing speech for decades, and in the past few years, they've gotten very good at it. Apple platforms already have an API for it. macOS 26 and iOS 26 introduced SpeechAnalyzer, Apple's newly introduced speech-to-text API. You add modules such as SpeechTranscriber and SpeechDetector to an analyzer, give it a file or a stream of audio buffers, and read results from async sequences as they arrive. AssetInventory installs the models, so your app decides when downloads happen.

    It's a well-designed API, but the only engine behind it is Apple's. AnySpeechRecognizer keeps the API and lets you choose the engine:.

    The package mirrors SpeechAnalyzer, SpeechTranscriber, DictationTranscriber, SpeechDetector, and AssetInventory, with Apple's Speech framework as the default engine. If your code uses that shared API, changing the import is enough. To use Parakeet instead, change only how you create the transcriber:.

    The steps for installing assets, running the analyzer, and reading results stay the same. The README has a complete example and lists the differences from Apple's framework.

    Sources indicate that parakeet v3 is NVIDIA's Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3. It's a polyglot: it recognizes 25 European languages and works out which one it's hearing, so you don't pass a locale.

    Parakeet Ultra is Moondream's post-trained take on v3. It was more accurate in most of our measurements.

    Parakeet Unified is NVIDIA's English-only Parakeet.

    All three Parakeets run on the package's own Core ML runtime, which supports file and live input, volatile results, word timing, and word confidence.

    Qwen3-ASR is Alibaba's speech model, in 0.6B and 1.7B sizes. It recognizes 30 languages and 22 Chinese dialects, including Mandarin, Cantonese, Japanese, and Korean, which Parakeet doesn't cover. It detects the language automatically, or you can set one:.

    Qwen3-ASR gives one final result for each segment of up to 40 seconds, without volatile results, word timing, or confidence. It runs on the GPU and is slower than Parakeet, so it's better suited to transcribing files than live input.

    To add another engine, implement SpeechRecognitionModel for its configuration and SpeechRecognitionExecutor for one module's session. The README includes a small provider that reports placeholder text to help you get started.

    To run these models in apps, we converted them to Core ML and published them on the Hub:.

    Each repository records its source checkpoint and a checksum for every file, and the package pins it to a fixed revision. The Parakeet repositories add an 8-second encoder for live input, which cuts live analysis time by about a third at the cost of a somewhat higher word error rate. The repository also has the conversion workflows, most of which follow FluidInference's mobius scripts, and checks each conversion against the original model.

    Downloads happen only when your app asks for them: about 600 MB for each Parakeet, plus about 590 MB for the live encoder, 0.9 to 2.4 GB for Qwen3-ASR, and about 250 MB for Sortformer. Files go in the standard Hugging Face cache, so a Mac app outside the sandbox shares them with Python and other Hugging Face tools.

    Sources indicate that when you transcribe a conversation, you often want to know who mentioned what. That's speaker diarization, and Apple's Speech framework doesn't have a module for it, so AnySpeechRecognizer adds one. SpeakerDiarizer runs NVIDIA's Streaming Sortformer on Core ML alongside an Apple or Parakeet transcriber, on the same timeline:.

    It has been revealed that the diarizer tracks up to four speakers, even when they talk over each other. A SpeakerTimeline collects its results and attributes each timed word to a speaker, so you can print a transcript by speaker turn. Like image support in AnyLanguageModel, this goes beyond what Apple's API offers today.

    In a recent development, the diarizer uses Sortformer v2 by default. You can also choose v2.1, which NVIDIA trained with more meeting data and which was more accurate on meetings in our measurements, too.

    It has been revealed that we measured the package with its hear command-line tool on an M4 Max Mac Studio with macOS 27.0.1. Here are the word error rates on LibriSpeech files of 3 to 8 minutes:.

    Parakeet transcribes an hour of audio in about 20 to 40 seconds from a file, or about 1.5 to 2.5 minutes live, with about 100 MB of memory once Core ML has compiled the model. Qwen3-ASR is much slower and needs a few gigabytes of memory. Meetings are hard for everyone: on AMI recordings, where people talk over each other, every engine we tested had a word error rate above 23%.

    These numbers come from one machine and a few datasets, so measure with your own hardware and audio. hear evaluate works on your own files, and the repository's natural-speech-eval.py tool reproduces these measurements. So far, we've tested only on macOS 27, not on an iPhone.

    Next, we'd like to add more engines, including Core AI on macOS 27 and iOS 27.

    Recent findings suggest that anyDecisionModel is a different story. There's no Apple framework to map onto, and decision models aren't newly introduced, exactly.

    It's only a decision model if it comes from the Décision region of France; otherwise, it's sparkling zero-shot classification.

    It has been revealed that what's new is the name, a lot of hype, and a crop of models trained to make decisions. We think that's where things are going, so we wanted a Swift API that's ready for them.

    Apps often ask language models to make decisions. Is this message urgent? Which team should handle this ticket? How frustrated is this customer? The usual approach is to prompt a language model and parse the text that it generates. That gives you one answer, but doesn't show the probabilities it assigned to the alternatives.

    Here's what a decision looks like in Swift:.

    urgent is a Double. team is a Choice containing the selected case, a probability for each option, and a confidence value. anger is a Score containing the expected level, a probability for each level, and a confidence value. Because Department conforms to Choosable, team.value is a Department that you can use in an exhaustive switch.

    If you've used Foundation Models or AnyLanguageModel, the model-and-session pattern will look familiar. A DecisionSession holds a single state, which can be text or JSON, and every question is about that state. Questions are independent: an answer never becomes input to a later question. To ask several questions at once, pass them to decide(_:) as a batch.

    For each question, the MLX backend builds a prompt with a one-token label for each allowed answer, then reads the probability of each label from one forward pass.

    Emoji Magnet is a macOS app with a text field above a pile of 343 emoji. Type a phrase, such as "things you wear", and the emoji that match rise out of the pile. Refine it to "things you wear in winter", and the emoji that no longer match fall back.

    The app has no built-in keyword rules; the model decides everything at inference time. When you pause typing, it asks the model one yes-or-no question for each emoji, for example:.

    Sources indicate that the session's state holds the phrase. The demo above uses the hosted Jev backend, which answers all 343 questions in one request, so the emoji settle in about half a second for each phrase. Without a TYPESAFE_AI_API_KEY, the app runs Qwen3 4B on your Mac with the MLX backend. That backend uses prefix caching to evaluate the state once, then answers 16 questions per forward pass. On an M4 Max, a group of 16 takes about 0.45 seconds after the model loads. A full pass over all 343 emoji takes about 10 seconds, and each group's results appear as soon as they arrive.

    Emoji Magnet is in the AnyDecisionModel-Examples repository.

    Reading next-token probabilities works with general-purpose language models, but those models weren't trained to make decisions. Cloudflare's Clef models are an example of a newer approach: a model with a trained decision head that turns a state and a schema of typed questions into decisions, returning probabilities for all allowed options across the questions in one forward pass. Clef-Flash is the 9B variant.

    AnyDecisionModel runs Clef-Flash on a Mac with MLX:.

    Sources indicate that you use the same sessions and questions, but MLXHeadDecisionModel reads each decision from Clef's trained decision head instead of from next-token probabilities. The 4-bit model is a 6.2 GB download, and its model card recommends a Mac with at least 16 GB of memory. Clef can read images and video, but this backend accepts only text and JSON states.

    Raw probabilities from language models are often overconfident. The local backends accept a Calibration, which applies a temperature to every answer and a bias to yes-or-no answers. Use separate datasets to fit the calibration and evaluate the results.

    Language models can also favor an option because of its position in a list. On the MLX, Core AI, and llama.cpp next-token backends, turn on rotationDebiasing to ask a choice question once for each rotation of the options and average the probabilities. That costs one prompt evaluation per rotation.

    According to recent reports, each local choice and score also includes a confidence value based on the entropy of its probabilities. It measures how concentrated the probabilities are, not whether the answer is right, so check the error rate on your own data before you pick a threshold. The next-token backends' diagnostics report how much probability the model assigned to the allowed answers. A low value means it assigned most of the probability elsewhere.

    AnyDecisionModel has six backends:.

    The next-token backends label answers "yes" and "no", A to Z, or 0 to 9, so a choice can have at most 26 options, and a score at most 10 levels. Decision heads have no such limit.

    Like AnyLanguageModel, the package uses Swift package traits. Without traits, it has no third-party dependencies. You get the core types and the Jev and Ollama backends, which also build on Linux. Enable the MLX, CoreAI, or Llama trait for the local backends.

    Both packages require Swift 6.2 or later and macOS 26 or iOS 26 or later. The Parakeet and Sortformer runtimes and the MLX backend require Apple silicon. AnyDecisionModel's MLX build tasks use Xcode's Swift 6.4 or later and the Metal toolchain; Core AI requires Xcode 27 and an OS 27 runtime.

    Add the packages to your Package.swift:.

    For now, AnyDecisionModel's CoreAI trait can't be combined with AnySpeechRecognizer, because coreai-kit 0.7.3 requires swift-huggingface below 1.0 and AnySpeechRecognizer requires 1.x.

    According to recent reports, each README has more examples and details about requirements and backends. AnySpeechRecognizer also includes a command-line tool, hear, that transcribes local files, labels their speakers, and evaluates the results. Every hear command requires --backend apple, --backend parakeet, or --backend qwen; run hear prepare with the same backend and model options before analysis to install the needed assets.

    Sources indicate that try them in your apps and tell us what works and what doesn't. Problems and pull requests are welcome on both repositories.

    Thanks to NVIDIA for Parakeet, Sortformer, and NeMo, to Moondream for Parakeet Ultra, to FluidInference, whose FluidAudio and mobius projects documented the conventions that the Parakeet runtime and the Core ML conversions follow, to Cloudflare for Clef, and to everyone who contributed to AnyLanguageModel, whose patterns both packages borrow.

Before the IPO, the tech giant had raised $141.1 billion of capital as of that date. Its multi-chip architecture spans AWS Trainium, Google TPUs, Nvidia GPUs and AMD GPUs.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Ginger VS Grammarly: When it comes to grammar checkers, Ginger and Grammarly are two of the most popular choices on the market.
    • Industry observers note that ginger VS Grammarly: When it comes to grammar checkers, Ginger and Grammarly are two of the most popular choices on the market.
    • If you are a writer, you must have heard of  Grammarly before.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Ginger VS Grammarly: When it comes to grammar checkers, Ginger and Grammarly are two of the most popular choices on the market. This article aims to highlight the specifics of each one so that you can make a more informed decision about the one you'll use.What is Grammarly?If you are a writer, you must have heard of  Grammarly before. Grammarly has over 10M people across the globe, it's probably the most popular AI writing enhancement tool, without a doubt. That's why there's a high chance that you already know about Grammarly.But today we are going to do a comparison between Ginger and Grammarly, So let's define Grammarly here. Like Ginger, Grammarly is an AI writing assistant that checks for grammatical errors, spellings, and punctuation. The free version covers the basics like identifying grammar and spelling mistakesWhile the Premium version offers a lot more functionality, it detects plagiarism in your content, suggests word choice, or adds fluency to it.Features of GrammarlyGrammarly detects basic to advance grammatical errors and also help you why this is an error and suggest to you how you can improve itCreate a personal dictionary Check to spell for American, British, Canadian, and Australian English.Understand inconsistencies. Detect unclear structure. Detect Plagiarism.Explore overuse of words and wordiness. Get to know about the improper tones. Discover the insensitive language aligns with your intent, audience, style, emotion, and more.What is Ginger Ginger is a writing enhancement tool that not only catches typos and grammatical mistakes but also suggests content improvements. As you type, it picks up on errors then indicates you what’s wrong, and suggests a fix.     Welcome Le Chonk: Mistral Large 4 on Hugging Face

    📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1609 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, mistral Large 4 (aka Le Chonk) is a multimodal, multilingual, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model from Mistral.
    • There are also GGUFs created by Unsloth and the llama.cpp team.
    • Sources indicate that mistral Large 4 is particularly strong for cybersecurity, coding agents, and multimodality.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, mistral Large 4 (aka Le Chonk) is a multimodal, multilingual, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model from Mistral. It takes text and images as input and generates text. It has about 1T total, 49B active parameter, and a context window of 1M tokens.

    The model is released in two official variants:.

    There are also GGUFs created by Unsloth and the llama.cpp team. It’s distributed under the Mistral Ecosystem Open-Weight License (an MIT derivative that establishes limitations for model-as-a-service offerings).

    Sources indicate that mistral Large 4 is particularly strong for cybersecurity, coding agents, and multimodality. In this post, we look at how the model works, its capabilities, architecture and more!

    Mistral Large 4 combines a large pool of experts with sparse attention and a Pixtral vision encoder. The language model selects a small group of experts for each token, while its attention indexer selects which earlier token positions to attend to. These are two different forms of sparsity, where one selects feed-forward networks, the other selects context positions.

    You can find all the checkpoints in the Mistral Large 4 collection.

    Mistral Large 4 scores 82% on the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index test that asks a model to reproduce a real vulnerability in open-source software and then patch the software. Mistral reports that several closed frontier models score near zero on the same test because they refuse to attempt the work. This is super important for defenders, because fixing a vulnerability usually requires reproducing the vulnerability. In Mistral’s internal testing, Mistral Large 4 was also useful for malware analysis, vulnerability prioritisation and writing detection rules, which the model was not explicitly trained for.

    Recent findings suggest that mistral mainly positions the model for defensive security work. Vulnerability research and incident response often appear like attacks in model input, so closed source filters can block them. A team that depends on an API can also lose access in the middle of an incident. Crucially, open weight models put both the usage policy and the deployment under the user’s control. That stated, the model still declines harmful requests: on cyber prompts from JailbreakBench, StrongREJECT and AgentHarm, its average refusal rate is higher than any other open weight model.

    It has been revealed that for community builders, an open weight model like Mistral Large 4 unlocks a load of downstream use cases. You could build your own cyber system around your code base, crash logs, and malware samples. For example, with TRL you could fine-tune smaller models from Mistral Large 4 traces patching your code base. In fact, reproduce-then-patch tasks use a verifiable reward, so it fits with RL environments that could be used to further RL smaller security models. Open weights also let researchers measure the model’s refusal behaviour directly instead of relying on the provider’s description.

    In short, cyber capabilities like ML4’s in the open are a huge boost for the community.

    We have interviewed Pierre Stock about the cyber capabilities of the model, you can watch it here.

    Industry observers note that mistral Large 4’s text decoder has 72 layers, a hidden dimension of 6,144, and 64 attention heads. Its attention blocks combine Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) with a DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) indexer (a direction in other models such as GLM 5.3). MLA keeps a compressed KV representation, and DSA selects up to 2,048 key positions for each query.

    It has been revealed that for each decoder block, there’s a 3:1 RoPE to NoPE pattern, i.e. 3 decoder layers employ RoPE and every fourth layer uses NoPE. The model also shares KV state across layers.The first decoder layer uses a dense feed-forward network. The other 71 layers use MoE blocks, in which a softmax router selects four of the 128 experts for each token. One shared expert always runs alongside the selected experts, for a total of 5 active experts per token.

    Regarding RoPE, Mistral uses LeRope, a YaRN-scaled RoPE with one learned multiplier per frequency.

    It has been revealed that mistral Large 4 employs a 1.6B Pixtral encoder. Pixtral has 30 layers, a hidden dimension of 2,048, and 16 attention heads. It uses 14 × 14 patches and a patch-merge projector with spatial merge size 2. You can see the encoder pipeline below.

    Mistral Large 4 delivers strong benchmark performance across coding, cybersecurity, multimodal understanding, and agentic workflows, positioning it as a competitive addition to the open-weight ecosystem. As of October 29, 2026, the model is the fifth best open weights model on Artificial Analysis Intelligence index.

    Industry observers note that on coding, ML4 achieves 61.7% on DeepSWE v1.1, 59.4% on SWE-Atlas-QnA, and 28.3% on Terminal-Bench 4. Its combined Coding Agent Index score of 49.8% places it ahead of DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813 and Qwen3.8 Max.

    Coding capabilities of ML4 extend to knowledge work, with 59.9% on AutomationBench and 1,393 Elo on AA-Briefcase, which evaluate business workflows and long-horizon professional tasks.

    In a recent development, cybersecurity is one of Mistral Large 4’s standout capabilities, with strong results across real-world vulnerability assessment and security competition tasks. Three benchmarks highlight the model’s cyber performance:.

    Recent findings suggest that mistral Large 4 also demonstrates 93.3% attack resistance on Lakera’s B3 benchmark, adding evidence of robustness against prompt-injection attacks. Beyond benchmarks, internal testing indicated promising results in malware analysis, vulnerability prioritization, and detection-rule generation.

    According to recent reports, mistral Large 4 is shipped with day-0 support for transformers, vLLM and llama.cpp. GGUF quants are available from GGUF and the llama.cpp team. We provide options to deploy remotely with Inference Endpoints, and use serverless inference through Inference Providers.

    It has been revealed that the Transformers implementation provides AutoModelForMultimodalLM, with AutoProcessor preparing the conversation and image inputs. Mistral Large 4 can take low, medium, high as reasoning effort. The default is high, and note that reasoning cannot be disabled, so using reasoning_effort: none would still use high.

The 2-bit quants run on a single Apple Silicon Ultra computer with 512 GB of unified RAM. The others require distributed inference. You can also run on multiple NVIDIA or AMD cards.

    Mistral Large 4 is also available on Inference Endpoints, with a ready-to-deploy recipe on 8 x NVIDIA H200 GPUs. The recipe runs vLLM with the FP8 weights split across all eight GPUs using tensor and expert parallelism, and uses the model's built-in DSpark draft head for faster generation through speculative decoding.     📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1570 w)
